Entropy–stable discontinuous Galerkin approximation with summation–by–parts property for the incompressible Navier–Stokes/Cahn–Hilliard system

Juan Manzanero    Gonzalo Rubio   
David A. Kopriva    Esteban Ferrer    Eusebio Valero E-mail: juan.manzanero@upm.es Affiliation: ETSIAE-UPM - School of Aeronautics, Universidad Politécnica de Madrid. Plaza Cardenal Cisneros 3, E-28040 Madrid, Spain. // Center for Computational Simulation, Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, Campus de Montegancedo, Boadilla del Monte, 28660, Madrid, Spain.
David A. Kopriva Department of Mathematics, Florida State University and Computational Science Research Center, San Diego State University.
Received: date / Accepted: date
Abstract

We develop an entropy stable two–phase incompressible Navier–Stokes/Cahn–Hilliard discontinuous Galerkin (DG) flow solver method. The model poses the Cahn–Hilliard equation as the phase field method, a skew–symmetric form of the momentum equation, and an artificial compressibility method to compute the pressure. We design the model so that it satisfies an entropy law, including free– and no–slip wall boundary conditions with non–zero wall contact angle. We then construct a high–order DG approximation of the model that satisfies the SBP–SAT property. With the help of a discrete stability analysis, the scheme has two modes: an entropy conserving approximation with central advective fluxes and the Bassi–Rebay 1 (BR1) method for diffusion, and an entropy stable approximation with an exact Riemann solver for advection and interface stabilization added to the BR1 method. The scheme is applicable to, and the stability proofs hold for, three–dimensional unstructured meshes with curvilinear hexahedral elements. We test the convergence of the schemes on a manufactured solution, and their robustness by solving a flow initialized from random numbers. In the latter, we find that a similar scheme that does not satisfy an entropy inequality had 30%\% probability to fail, while the entropy stable scheme never does. We also solve the static and rising bubble test problems, and to challenge the solver capabilities we compute a three–dimensional pipe flow in the annular regime.

Keywords: 
Navier–Stokes Cahn–Hilliard Computational fluid dynamics High-Order methods Discontinuous Galerkin SBP–SAT.

1 Introduction

The study of multiphase flows is of broad interest, from both scientific and industrial perspectives. In particular, the oil industry investigates two–phase flows of immiscible fluids (e.g. oil and water). Without mixing, the typical flow configuration is the segregation of the two fluids, separated by a thin interfacial region that behaves like a permeable membrane. At the interface of two dissimilar fluids, the forces acting on the molecules of each of these fluids are not the same as within each phase and generate interfacial tension.

Among the various techniques to approach the solution of immiscible two–phase flows, one finds two broad categories: sharp and diffuse interface models. In the former, the interface is considered infinitely thin, and acts as a physical boundary condition where the two fluids are coupled and balanced by interfacial forces [1]. An example of a sharp interface model is the level–set method [2], where the interface is tracked by an additional variable advected by the flow velocity field.

Diffuse interface approaches, however, regularize the problem with the introduction of an interface with non–zero thickness and a smooth transition of thermodynamic variables between both fluids. This time, interfacial forces (which in the sharp interface approach are delta functions applied at the interface) are transformed to body forces whose effect is concentrated at the interface [3].

In this work we study the diffuse interface model of Cahn–Hilliard [4, 5] combined with the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations with variable density and artificial (also called pseudo) compressibility [6]. A review of alternate Navier–Stokes/Cahn–Hilliard models can be found in [7].

We discretize the system of partial differential equations that represents the model with a high–order Discontinuous Galerkin Spectral Element Method (DGSEM). The DGSEM allows for arbitrary order of accuracy and can represent complex geometries through the use of unstructured meshes with curvilinear elements. Here, we develop an entropy–stable discretization, which enhances its robustness and enables the industrialization of the method.

This work is the third on a roadmap to obtain an entropy stable multiphase solver. In [8], we developed a free–energy stable discretization of the Cahn–Hilliard equation, while in [9] we derived an entropy–stable approximation of the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations with artificial compressibility. We combine the developments in those previous papers to construct an entropy–stable DG approximation of the incompressible Navier–Stokes/Cahn–Hilliard system.

As in [8, 9], the method is a nodal DG approximation with Gauss–Lobatto points, which satisfies the summation–by–parts simultaneous–aproximation–term (SBP–SAT) property [10, 11]. The SBP–SAT property satisfied by the Gauss–Lobatto variant of the DGSEM allows us to mimic the continuous entropy analysis semi–discretely (i.e. discrete in space, continuous in time). The SBP-SAT property originated with finite difference methods [10, 11, 12], and has been exploited in recent years to obtain entropy–stable DG schemes for the linear advection equation [13, 14], Burgers equation [15, 16], shallow water equations [17], Euler and Navier–Stokes equations [18, 16, 9], the magneto–hydrodynamics equations [19], and the Cahn–Hilliard equation [8] among others. Although we develop a DG approximation, the approach taken here can be applied to any discretization that satisfies the SBP–SAT property (e.g. finite difference).

An entropy–stable approximation requires that the continuous system of partial differential equations satisfies an entropy law. When the density is allowed to vary between the two fluids in a multiphase flow, as opposed to the more traditional Model H [20] with constant density, the design of an entropy–stable scheme requires care. The variable density compromises the formulation used for the momentum equation [21]. Two main approaches to the design of a variable density entropy–stable approximation are commonly adopted: to use a skew–symmetric version of the momentum equation [22], or to augment the momentum equation with an additional diffusive flux that depends on the density difference [23, 24].

The addition of the artificial compressibility model, where a divergence–free velocity is not strictly enforced, completes the formulation used for the body interfacial forces. Without proper choices, terms proportional to ∇→⋅u→\svec{\nabla}\cdot\svec{u}, which can not be neglected nor bounded, might appear in the entopy equation. With the proper choices, we confirm that the entropy of the Navier–Stokes/Cahn–Hilliard system obeys the Onsager principle; the total entropy is the sum of the entropy of the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, plus the free–energy of the Cahn–Hilliard equation [4]. In [9] we derived a mathematical entropy of the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations with artificial compressibility as the sum of the traditional kinetic energy, plus an additional energy term that accounts for compressibility effects. As a result, the total entropy becomes the sum of the kinetic energy, the artificial compressibility energy, and the free–energy.

In this paper we construct a multiphase approximation that is appropriate to solve typical applications in the oil industry. An example is the transport of crude oil in pipes, where the flow of oil and water is solved under high Reynolds number conditions. Since one desires to keep the mesh and degrees of freedom as low as possible, the flow configuration is often under–resolved. Under these circumstances, a robust method that is provably stable is attractive, as it avoids aliasing driven numerical instabilities that might lead to numerical divergence [14].

The rest of this work is organized as follows: in Sec. 2 we describe the incompressible Navier–Stokes/Cahn–Hilliard model, with the continuous entropy analysis in Sec. 2.1. The construction of the discrete DG approximation is described in Sec.3. Then, the semi–discrete stability analysis of the approximation is performed in Sec. 4, for which a summary can be found in Sec. 4.5. Lastly, we provide numerical experiments in Sec. 5 that assess both the accuracy and robustness of the method. We solve a manufactured solution convergence analysis in Sec. 5.1, and an assessment of the robustness solving a random initial condition in Sec. 5.2. Then, we solve classic static and rising bubble test problems in Sec. 5.3 and Sec. 5.4 respectively. Lastly, in Sec. 5.5 we challenge the technique by solving a multiphase pipe in the annular flow regime. Conclusions and discussions can be found in Sec. 6.

2 Governing equations. Continuous entropy analysis

In this section we describe a model that combines the incompressible Navier–Stokes and the Cahn–Hilliard equations, which we will refer to as iNS/CH. In the single phase variable density incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, the density ρ⁡(x→,t)\rho(\svec{x},t) is an independent variable that satisfies the continuity equation (see [22, 25, 9]),

ρt+∇→⋅(ρ​u→)=0,\rho_{t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\rho\svec{u}\right)=0, (1)

where u→​(x→,t)=(u,v,w)\svec{u}(\svec{x},t)=\left(u,v,w\right) is the velocity field. In the two–phase iNS/CH system, however, the density is computed from the concentration c⁡(x→,t)c(\svec{x},t) of the two fluids [3],

ρ=ρ⁡(c)=ρ1​c+ρ2​(1−c),\rho=\rho(c)=\rho_{1}c+\rho_{2}(1-c), (2)

where ρ1,2\rho_{1,2} are the densities of fluids 1 and 2, respectively, which are constant in space and time.

In phase field methods, an advection–diffusion equation drives the concentration. Among the model choices, we pick the Cahn–Hilliard equation [4, 5],

ct+∇→⋅(c​u→)=M0​∇→2​μ.c_{t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(c\svec{u}\right)=M_{0}\svec{\nabla}^{2}\mu. (3)

In (3), μ\mu is the chemical potential,

μ=⁡d​f0​(c)⁡d​c−32​σ​ε​∇→2​c,\mu=\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}f_{0}(c)}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}c}-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\svec{\nabla}^{2}c, (4)

where f0​(c)f_{0}(c) is the chemical free–energy,

f0=12​σε​c2​(1−c)2,f_{0}=\frac{12\sigma}{\varepsilon}c^{2}(1-c)^{2}, (5)

σ\sigma is the coefficient of interface tension between the fluids, ε\varepsilon is the interface width, and M0M_{0} is the mobility, computed in this work with the chemical characteristic time, tCHt_{\mathrm{CH}}, as

M0=εσ​tCH.M_{0}=\frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma t_{\mathrm{CH}}}. (6)

The parameters σ\sigma, ε\varepsilon, M0M_{0}, and tCHt_{\mathrm{CH}} are positive constants. The Cahn–Hilliard equation (3), with the chemical potential definition (4), has an associated free–energy

ℱ⁡(c,∇→​c)=f0​(c)+34​σ​ε​|∇→​c|2.\mathcal{F}(c,\svec{\nabla}c)=f_{0}(c)+\frac{3}{4}\sigma\varepsilon|\svec{\nabla}c|^{2}. (7)

The velocity field is computed from the momentum equation. If one considers that the continuity equation (1) holds, the conservative,

(ρ​u→)t+∇→⋅(ρ​u→​u→)=−∇→​ps−∇→⋅(∇→​c⊗∂ℱ∂∇→​c)+∇→⋅(η⁡(∇→​u→+∇→​u→T))+ρ​g→,\left(\rho\svec{u}\right)_{t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\rho\svec{u}\svec{u}\right)=-\svec{\nabla}p_{s}-\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\svec{\nabla}c\otimes\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\svec{\nabla}c}\right)+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\eta\left(\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}+\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}^{T}\right)\right)+\rho\svec{g}, (8)

non–conservative,

ρ​(u→)t+ρ​u→⋅∇→​u→=−∇→​ps−∇→⋅(∇→​c⊗∂ℱ∂∇→​c)+∇→⋅(η⁡(∇→​u→+∇→​u→T))+ρ​g→,\rho\left(\svec{u}\right)_{t}+\rho\svec{u}\cdot\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}=-\svec{\nabla}p_{s}-\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\svec{\nabla}c\otimes\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\svec{\nabla}c}\right)+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\eta\left(\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}+\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}^{T}\right)\right)+\rho\svec{g}, (9)

and skew–symmetric

12​(ρ​u→)t+12​ρ​(u→)t+∇→⋅(12​ρ​u→​u→)+12​ρ​u→⋅∇→​u→=−∇→​ps−∇→⋅(∇→​c⊗∂ℱ∂∇→​c)+∇→⋅(η⁡(∇→​u→+∇→​u→T))+ρ​g→,\frac{1}{2}\left(\rho\svec{u}\right)_{t}+\frac{1}{2}\rho\left(\svec{u}\right)_{t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho\svec{u}\svec{u}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\rho\svec{u}\cdot\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}=-\svec{\nabla}p_{s}-\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\svec{\nabla}c\otimes\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\svec{\nabla}c}\right)+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\eta\left(\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}+\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}^{T}\right)\right)+\rho\svec{g}, (10)

forms of the momentum equation are identical in the continuous setting. However, since the density does not satisfy the continuity equation (1), but rather the compatibility condition (2), the three forms (8), (9) and (10) are no longer equivalent. In this situation, the momentum equation is frozen as one of the three forms. Following [22, 21], we choose the skew–symmetric version of the momentum (10) since is the only one that satisfies an entropy inequality for any positive density field. (An alternative that produces an entropy–stable scheme for the iNS/CH system is to include a relative flux in the momentum equation that models the diffusion of the components [26].) We use the chain rule in time to perform an additional manipulation on the time derivative of (10) and obtain the momentum form by Guermond et al. [22],

ρ​(ρ​u→)t+∇→⋅(12​ρ​u→​u→)+12​ρ​u→⋅∇→​u→=−∇→​ps−∇→⋅(∇→​c⊗∂ℱ∂∇→​c)+∇→⋅(η⁡(∇→​u→+∇→​u→T))+ρ​g→.\sqrt{\rho}\left(\sqrt{\rho}\svec{u}\right)_{t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho\svec{u}\svec{u}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\rho\svec{u}\cdot\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}=-\svec{\nabla}p_{s}-\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\svec{\nabla}c\otimes\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\svec{\nabla}c}\right)+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\eta\left(\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}+\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}^{T}\right)\right)+\rho\svec{g}. (11)

In (11), ps​(x→,t)p_{s}\left(\svec{x},t\right) is the static pressure. The second term is the body force approximation of the capillary pressure [3],

p→c=−∇→⋅(∇→c⊗∂ℱ∂∇→​c)=−32σε∇→⋅(∇→c⊗∇→c).\svec{p}_{c}=-\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\svec{\nabla}c\otimes\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\svec{\nabla}c}\right)=-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\svec{\nabla}c\otimes\svec{\nabla}c\right). (12)

Finally η\eta is the viscosity, computed from the concentration cc and the viscosities of fluids 1 and 2, η1,2\eta_{1,2},

η=η⁡(c)=η1​c+η2​(1−c).\eta=\eta(c)=\eta_{1}c+\eta_{2}\left(1-c\right). (13)

As in [3], we write the capillary pressure more conveniently. Applying the derivative product rule,

p→c=−32​σ​ε​(∇→2​c​∇→​c+∇→​(12​|∇→​c|2)),\svec{p}_{c}=-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\left(\svec{\nabla}^{2}c\svec{\nabla}c+\svec{\nabla}\left(\frac{1}{2}|\svec{\nabla}c|^{2}\right)\right), (14)

and adding and subtracting the term ∇→​f0=f0′​(c)​∇→​c\svec{\nabla}f_{0}=f^{\prime}_{0}(c)\svec{\nabla}c, we can rewrite the expression for the body force as

p→c=(f0′​(c)−32​σ​ε​∇→2​c)​∇→​c−∇→​(f0​(c)+34​σ​ε​|∇→​c|2)=μ​∇→​c−∇→​ℱ=−c​∇→​μ−∇→​(ℱ−μ​c).\svec{p}_{c}=\left(f^{\prime}_{0}(c)-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\svec{\nabla}^{2}c\right)\svec{\nabla}c-\svec{\nabla}\left(f_{0}(c)+\frac{3}{4}\sigma\varepsilon|\svec{\nabla}c|^{2}\right)=\mu\svec{\nabla}c-\svec{\nabla}\mathcal{F}=-c\svec{\nabla}\mu-\svec{\nabla}\left(\mathcal{F}-\mu c\right). (15)

In the last form, an additional application of the product derivative rule for the first term has been performed. Eq. (15) represents equivalent expressions of the capillary pressure (12), the last form being the one adopted here. The first term of the last form, −c​∇→​μ-c\svec{\nabla}\mu, is a non–conservative term, and the second, −∇→​(ℱ−μ​c)-\svec{\nabla}\left(\mathcal{F}-\mu c\right), is combined with the static pressure gradient to define an auxiliary pressure

p=ps+ℱ−μ​c.p=p_{s}+\mathcal{F}-\mu c. (16)

With all of these manipulations, we get the final expression of the momentum equation,

ρ​(ρ​u→)t+∇→⋅(12​ρ​u→​u→)+12​ρ​u→⋅∇→​u→+c​∇→​μ=−∇→​p+∇→⋅(η⁡(∇→​u→+∇→​u→T))+ρ​g→.\sqrt{\rho}\left(\sqrt{\rho}\svec{u}\right)_{t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho\svec{u}\svec{u}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\rho\svec{u}\cdot\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}+c\svec{\nabla}\mu=-\svec{\nabla}p+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\eta\left(\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}+\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}^{T}\right)\right)+\rho\svec{g}. (17)

Many authors have explored how to relax the incompressibility constraint ∇→⋅u→=0\svec{\nabla}\cdot\svec{u}=0 in Navier–Stokes and Navier–Stokes/Cahn–Hilliard systems by using the artificial (or pseudo) compressibility method [6, 27, 28, 29]. We use the time derivative of the pressure [27, 25, 9],

pt+ρ0​c02​∇→⋅u→=0,p_{t}+\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}\svec{\nabla}\cdot\svec{u}=0, (18)

where c0c_{0} is the artificial sound speed, and ρ0=max⁡(ρ1,ρ2)\rho_{0}=\max\left(\rho_{1},\rho_{2}\right).

Remark 1

Alternatively, one can take the time derivative of the pressure Laplacian [6, 21, 30],

−∇→2​pt+ρ0​c02​∇→⋅u→=0.-\svec{\nabla}^{2}p_{t}+\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}\svec{\nabla}\cdot\svec{u}=0. (19)

Since both models share the same velocity divergence term, we can modify the proofs of stability for the approximation of (18) and study the approximation of the second model (19). We do so in Appendix A. The use of the Laplacian of the pressure leads to a more complicated implicit implementation, so for that scheme we include only the stability proof in this paper.

The combination of (3), (17) and (18) is the iNS/CH system studied in this paper. The coupling between the Cahn–Hilliard equation and the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations is two–way, through the compatibility conditions (2), (13), and the capillary pressure. We note that even in the continuous setting, the momentum is not conserved because of the choice of the skew–symmetric form (17). Although one can argue about the physical implications, we note that the capillary force is a non–conservative term as well, so momentum conservation is not guaranteed in any of the forms (8), (9), and (17). Alternative incompressible Navier–Stokes/Cahn–Hilliard discretizations using the skew–symmetric form of the momentum equation can be found in [31, 21].

To simplify the notation, we write the iNS/CH system as a general advection–diffusion equation,

where,

𝖲=sym⁡(∇→​u→)=12​(∇→​u→+∇→​u→T),\mathsf{S}=\mathrm{sym}\left(\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}+\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}^{T}\right), (21)

Note that we have grouped the velocity divergence in the artificial compressibility equation (18) into the non–conservative terms. Although treating the velocity divergence as conservative or non–conservative is equivalent, the latter makes it easier to show stability.

We adopt the notation in [16] to work with vectors of different nature. We define space vectors (e.g. x→=(x,y,z)∈ℝ3\svec{x}=\left(x,y,z\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}) with an arrow on top, and state vectors (e.g. 𝐪=(c,ρ​u→,p)∈ℝ5\mathbf{q}=\left(c,\sqrt{\rho}\svec{u},p\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{5}) in bold. and define the operator Υ\Upsilon that transforms a 5×35\times 3 (state–space) matrix into a 15×115\times 1 block vector,

𝐟↔=Υ⁡(f1g1h1f2g2h2f3g3h3f4g4h4f5g5h5)=(𝐟𝐠𝐡).\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}=\Upsilon\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}f_{1}&g_{1}&h_{1}\\ f_{2}&g_{2}&h_{2}\\ f_{3}&g_{3}&h_{3}\\ f_{4}&g_{4}&h_{4}\\ f_{5}&g_{5}&h_{5}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\mathbf{f}\\ \mathbf{g}\\ \mathbf{h}\end{array}\right). (23)

This notation allows us to define products of state, space, and block vectors,

𝐟↔⋅𝐠↔=∑i=13𝐟iT​𝐠i,g→⋅𝐟↔=∑i=13gi​𝐟i,g→​𝐟=(g1​𝐟g2​𝐟g3​𝐟).\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{g}}=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\mathbf{f}_{i}^{T}\mathbf{g}_{i},~~\svec{g}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}=\sum_{i=1}^{3}g_{i}\mathbf{f}_{i},~~\svec{g}\mathbf{f}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}g_{1}\mathbf{f}\\ g_{2}\mathbf{f}\\ g_{3}\mathbf{f}\end{array}\right). (24)

We can then define the divergence and gradient operators using (24),

∇→⋅𝐟↔=∑i=13∂𝐟i∂xi,∇→​𝐪=(𝐪x𝐪y𝐪z).\svec{\nabla}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\frac{\partial\mathbf{f}_{i}}{\partial x_{i}},~~\svec{\nabla}\mathbf{q}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\mathbf{q}_{x}\\ \mathbf{q}_{y}\\ \mathbf{q}_{z}\end{array}\right). (25)

Lastly, we refer to state matrices (i.e. 5×55\times 5 matrices) with an underline, e.g. 𝐁¯\underline{\mathbf{B}}, which can be combined to construct a block matrix,

ℬ=(𝐁¯11𝐁¯12𝐁¯13𝐁¯21𝐁¯22𝐁¯23𝐁¯31𝐁¯32𝐁¯33).\mathcal{B}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}\underline{\mathbf{B}}_{11}&\underline{\mathbf{B}}_{12}&\underline{\mathbf{B}}_{13}\\ \underline{\mathbf{B}}_{21}&\underline{\mathbf{B}}_{22}&\underline{\mathbf{B}}_{23}\\ \underline{\mathbf{B}}_{31}&\underline{\mathbf{B}}_{32}&\underline{\mathbf{B}}_{33}\end{array}\right). (26)

Block matrices can be directly multiplied to a block vector to obtain another block vector. For instance, to perform a matrix multiplication in space (e.g. a rotation),

g→=𝖬​f→,\svec{g}=\mathsf{M}\svec{f}, (27)

for each of the variables in the state vector, we construct the block matrix version of 𝖬\mathsf{M} (𝐈¯5\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5} is the 5×55\times 5 identity matrix),

ℳ=(M11​𝐈¯5M12​𝐈¯5M13​𝐈¯5M21​𝐈¯5M22​𝐈¯5M23​𝐈¯5M31​𝐈¯5M32​𝐈¯5M33​𝐈¯5),\mathcal{M}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}M_{11}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}&M_{12}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}&M_{13}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}\\ M_{21}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}&M_{22}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}&M_{23}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}\\ M_{31}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}&M_{32}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}&M_{33}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}\end{array}\right), (28)

so that we can compactly write

𝐠↔=ℳ​𝐟↔.\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{g}}=\mathcal{M}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}. (29)

For more details, see [16].

The notation introduced above makes it possible to write the iNS/CH system (20) compactly in the form of a general advection–diffusion equation,

𝐦¯​𝐪t+∇→⋅𝐟↔e​(𝐪)+∑m=15ϕ↔m​(𝐪)⋅∇→​wm=∇→⋅𝐟↔v​(𝐪,∇→​𝐰)+𝐬⁡(𝐪),\underline{\mathbf{m}}\mathbf{q}_{t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}\left(\mathbf{q}\right)+\sum_{m=1}^{5}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{m}\left(\mathbf{q}\right)\cdot\svec{\nabla}w_{m}=\svec{\nabla}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{v}\left(\mathbf{q},\svec{\nabla}\mathbf{w}\right)+\mathbf{s}\left(\mathbf{q}\right), (30)

with state vector 𝐪=(c,ρ​u→,p)\mathbf{q}=\left(c,\sqrt{\rho}\svec{u},p\right), gradient variables vector 𝐰=(w1,w2,…,w5)=(μ,u→,p)\mathbf{w}=\left(w_{1},w_{2},...,w_{5}\right)=\left(\mu,\svec{u},p\right), mass matrix 𝐦¯\underline{\mathbf{m}},

𝐦¯=(1000ρ​𝖨30001),\underline{\mathbf{m}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&0&0\\ 0&\sqrt{\rho}\mathsf{I}_{3}&0\\ 0&0&1\end{array}\right), (31)

inviscid fluxes 𝐟↔e​(𝐪)\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}\left(\mathbf{q}\right),

𝐟e,1=𝐟e=(c​uρ​u2+pρ​u​vρ​u​w0),𝐟e,2=𝐠e=(c​vρ​u​vρ​v2+pρ​v​w0),𝐟e,3=𝐡e=(c​wρ​u​wρ​v​wρ​w2+p0),\mathbf{f}_{e,1}=\mathbf{f}_{e}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}cu\\ \rho u^{2}+p\\ \rho uv\\ \rho uw\\ 0\end{array}\right),~~\mathbf{f}_{e,2}=\mathbf{g}_{e}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}cv\\ \rho uv\\ \rho v^{2}+p\\ \rho vw\\ 0\end{array}\right),~~\mathbf{f}_{e,3}=\mathbf{h}_{e}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}cw\\ \rho uw\\ \rho vw\\ \rho w^{2}+p\\ 0\end{array}\right), (32)

non–conservative term coefficients ϕ↔m​(𝐪)\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{m}\left(\mathbf{q}\right),

ϕ↔1=Υ⁡(0c​e→1c​e→2c​e→30),ϕ↔2=Υ⁡(012​ρ​u→00ρ0​c02​e→1),ϕ↔3=Υ​(0012​ρ​u→0ρ0​c02​e→2),ϕ↔4=Υ⁡(00012​ρ​u→ρ0​c02​e→3),ϕ↔5=Υ​(00000),\begin{split}&\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{1}=\Upsilon\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ c\svec{e}_{1}\\ c\svec{e}_{2}\\ c\svec{e}_{3}\\ 0\end{array}\right),~~\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{2}=\Upsilon\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho\svec{u}\\ 0\\ 0\\ \rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}\svec{e}_{1}\end{array}\right),~~\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{3}=\Upsilon\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ 0\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho\svec{u}\\ 0\\ \rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}\svec{e}_{2}\end{array}\right),\\ &\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{4}=\Upsilon\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ 0\\ 0\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho\svec{u}\\ \rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}\svec{e}_{3}\end{array}\right),~~\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{5}=\Upsilon\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ 0\\ 0\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right),\end{split} (33)

viscous fluxes 𝐟↔v​(∇→​𝐰)\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{v}\left(\svec{\nabla}\mathbf{w}\right),

𝐟v,1=𝐟v=(M0​μx2​η​𝖲112​η​𝖲212​η​𝖲310),𝐟v,2=𝐠v=(M0​μy2​η​𝖲122​η​𝖲222​η​𝖲320),𝐟v,3=𝐡v=(M0​μz2​η​𝖲132​η​𝖲232​η​𝖲330),\mathbf{f}_{v,1}=\mathbf{f}_{v}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}M_{0}\mu_{x}\\ 2\eta\mathsf{S}_{11}\\ 2\eta\mathsf{S}_{21}\\ 2\eta\mathsf{S}_{31}\\ 0\end{array}\right),~~\mathbf{f}_{v,2}=\mathbf{g}_{v}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}M_{0}\mu_{y}\\ 2\eta\mathsf{S}_{12}\\ 2\eta\mathsf{S}_{22}\\ 2\eta\mathsf{S}_{32}\\ 0\end{array}\right),~~\mathbf{f}_{v,3}=\mathbf{h}_{v}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}M_{0}\mu_{z}\\ 2\eta\mathsf{S}_{13}\\ 2\eta\mathsf{S}_{23}\\ 2\eta\mathsf{S}_{33}\\ 0\end{array}\right), (34)

and source term 𝐬⁡(𝐪)=(0,ρ​g→,0)\mathbf{s}\left(\mathbf{q}\right)=\left(0,\rho\svec{g},0\right).

An attractive property of the iNS/CH system from the point of view of computational efficiency is that the same gradient variables 𝐰\mathbf{w} are used in both the non–conservative terms and the viscous fluxes. Moreover, these gradient variables will be shown to be the entropy variables associated with the mathematical entropy in Section 2.1. Additionally, recall that the velocity divergence from the artificial compressibility equation (18) was grouped into the non–conservative terms since it is beneficial when proving stability.

2.1 Entropy analysis of the iNS/CH system

The entropy analysis rests on the existence of a pair ℰ⁡(𝐪)\mathcal{E}\left(\mathbf{q}\right) (mathematical entropy) and 𝐰\mathbf{w} (entropy variables) that contract the system of equations (30) into a conservation law [32],

𝐰T(𝐦¯​𝐪t+∇→⋅𝐟↔e​(𝐪)+∑m=15ϕ↔m​(𝐪)⋅∇→​wm−∇→⋅𝐟↔v​(𝐪,∇→​𝐰))=ℰt+∇⋅f→ℰ+∇𝐰T⋅𝐟↔v=0,\begin{split}\mathbf{w}^{T}&\left(\underline{\mathbf{m}}\mathbf{q}_{t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}\left(\mathbf{q}\right)+\sum_{m=1}^{5}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{m}\left(\mathbf{q}\right)\cdot\svec{\nabla}w_{m}-\svec{\nabla}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{v}\left(\mathbf{q},\svec{\nabla}\mathbf{w}\right)\right)\\ &=\mathcal{E}_{t}+\mathbf{\nabla}\cdot\svec{f}^{\mathcal{E}}+\mathbf{\nabla}\mathbf{w}^{T}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{v}=0,\end{split} (35)

with an entropy flux f→ℰ\svec{f}^{\mathcal{E}}, and a viscous dissipative contribution,

∇→​𝐰T⋅𝐟↔v⩾0.\svec{\nabla}\mathbf{w}^{T}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{v}\geqslant 0. (36)

The difference between the usual entropy analysis [32, 11, 11] and this work is that we will incorporate the Cahn–Hilliard free–energy into the mathematical entropy, which makes it depend not only on the solution, but also its gradient. To obtain the entropy of the iNS/CH system, we add the Cahn–Hilliard free–energy ℱ\mathcal{F} to the incompressible NSE entropy defined in [9]. The latter combines the traditional kinetic energy 𝒦\mathcal{K} with an extra energy term due to the artificial compressibility ℰAC\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{AC}}. For the iNS/CH system, the total entropy is,

ℰ=ℱ⁡(c,∇→​c)+𝒦⁡(ρ​u→)+ℰAC​(p)=f0​(c)+34​σ​ε​|∇→​c|2+12​ρ​vt​o​t2+p22​ρ0​c02⩾0,\begin{split}\mathcal{E}&=\mathcal{F}(c,\svec{\nabla}c)+\mathcal{K}\left(\sqrt{\rho}\svec{u}\right)+\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{AC}}(p)\\ &=f_{0}(c)+\frac{3}{4}\sigma\varepsilon|\svec{\nabla}c|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{tot}^{2}+\frac{p^{2}}{2\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}}\geqslant 0,\end{split} (37)

where vt​o​t2=u2+v2+w2v_{tot}^{2}=u^{2}+v^{2}+w^{2} is the square of the total speed. Eq. (37) assumes positivity on the density ρ\rho, which is ensured by limiting the maximum and minimum density values used in the momentum equation with a simple cutoff,

ρ⁡(c^)=ρ1​c^+ρ2​(1−c^),c^=min⁡(max⁡(c,0),1).\rho\left(\hat{c}\right)=\rho_{1}\hat{c}+\rho_{2}\left(1-\hat{c}\right),~~\hat{c}=\min\left(\max\left(c,0\right),1\right). (38)

We find a set of entropy variables 𝐰\mathbf{w} that contracts the time derivative of the state vector, 𝐪t\mathbf{q}_{t}, into the time derivative of the entropy ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t}, plus an additional divergence term of a time derivative flux f→tℰ\svec{f}_{t}^{\mathcal{E}},

𝐰T​𝐦¯​𝐪t=ℰt+∇→⋅f→tℰ.\mathbf{w}^{T}\underline{\mathbf{m}}\mathbf{q}_{t}=\mathcal{E}_{t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\svec{f}_{t}^{\mathcal{E}}. (39)

To do so, we compute the time derivative of the entropy (37),

ℰt=f0′(c)ct+32σε∇c⋅∇ct+ρu→⋅(ρu→)t+p​ptρ0​c02=(f0′​(c)−32​σ​ε​∇→2​c)​ct+∇→⋅(32​σ​ε​ct​∇→​c)+ρ​u→⋅(ρ​u→)t+p​ptρ0​c02=μ​ct+∇→⋅(32​σ​ε​ct​∇→​c)+ρ​u​(ρ​u)t+ρ​v​(ρ​v)t+ρ​w​(ρ​w)t+p​ptρ0​c02,\begin{split}\mathcal{E}_{t}&=f_{0}^{\prime}(c)c_{t}+\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\nabla c\cdot\nabla c_{t}+\sqrt{\rho}\svec{u}\cdot\left(\sqrt{\rho}\svec{u}\right)_{t}+\frac{pp_{t}}{\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}}\\ &=\left(f_{0}^{\prime}(c)-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\svec{\nabla}^{2}c\right)c_{t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon c_{t}\svec{\nabla}c\right)+\sqrt{\rho}\svec{u}\cdot\left(\sqrt{\rho}\svec{u}\right)_{t}+\frac{pp_{t}}{\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}}\\ &=\mu c_{t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon c_{t}\svec{\nabla}c\right)+\sqrt{\rho}u\left(\sqrt{\rho}u\right)_{t}+\sqrt{\rho}v\left(\sqrt{\rho}v\right)_{t}+\sqrt{\rho}w\left(\sqrt{\rho}w\right)_{t}+\frac{pp_{t}}{\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}},\end{split} (40)

and the product of the entropy variables with the time derivative of the state vector,

w1​ct+ρ​w2​(ρ​u)t+ρ​w3​(ρ​v)t+ρ​w4​(ρ​w)t+w5​pt.w_{1}c_{t}+\sqrt{\rho}w_{2}\left(\sqrt{\rho}u\right)_{t}+\sqrt{\rho}w_{3}\left(\sqrt{\rho}v\right)_{t}+\sqrt{\rho}w_{4}\left(\sqrt{\rho}w\right)_{t}+w_{5}p_{t}. (41)

Thus, we replace (40) and (41) in (39) and rearrange,

(w1−μ)​ct+ρ​(w2−u)​(ρ​u)t+ρ​(w3−v)​(ρ​v)t+ρ​(w4−w)​(ρ​w)t+(w5−pρ0​c02)​pt=∇→⋅(f→tℰ+32​σ​ε​ct​∇→​c),\begin{split}\left(w_{1}-\mu\right)c_{t}&+\sqrt{\rho}\left(w_{2}-u\right)\left(\sqrt{\rho}u\right)_{t}+\sqrt{\rho}\left(w_{3}-v\right)\left(\sqrt{\rho}v\right)_{t}+\sqrt{\rho}\left(w_{4}-w\right)\left(\sqrt{\rho}w\right)_{t}\\ &+\left(w_{5}-\frac{p}{\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}}\right)p_{t}=\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\svec{f}_{t}^{\mathcal{E}}+\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon c_{t}\svec{\nabla}c\right),\end{split} (42)

to extract the entropy variables 𝐰\mathbf{w} and time entropy flux f→tℰ\svec{f}_{t}^{\mathcal{E}}

𝐰=(μ,u,v,w,pρ0​c02),f→tℰ=−32​σ​ε​ct​∇→​c.\mathbf{w}=\left(\mu,u,v,w,\frac{p}{\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}}\right),~~\svec{f}_{t}^{\mathcal{E}}=-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon c_{t}\svec{\nabla}c. (43)

Note that the minimum of the entropy is found when all the entropy variables are zero.

The contraction of the inviscid fluxes rests on one property to be satisfied by the inviscid fluxes and the non–conservative terms.

Property 1

If inviscid fluxes, 𝐟↔e\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}, and non–conservative terms coefficients, ϕ↔m\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{m}, satisfy

𝐞mT​𝐟↔e=𝐰T​ϕ↔m,\mathbf{e}_{m}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}=\mathbf{w}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\phi}}_{m}, (44)

where 𝐞m\mathbf{e}_{m} is the state unit vector along the mm–th state variable, then the entropy variables automatically contract the inviscid fluxes, and the entropy flux is computed as

f→eℰ=𝐰T​𝐟↔e.\svec{f}_{e}^{\mathcal{E}}=\mathbf{w}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}. (45)

To show the contraction property (44), we multiply the divergence of the inviscid fluxes by the entropy variables, apply the derivative product rule, and write the second scalar product as the sum of the product of the five state components. Lastly we use (44) and (45) to see that

𝐰T​∇→⋅𝐟↔e=∇→⋅(𝐰T𝐟↔e)−∇𝐰T⋅𝐟↔e=∇→⋅(𝐰T𝐟↔e)−∑m=15𝐞Tm𝐟↔e⋅∇→wm=∇→⋅f→eℰ−∑m=15𝐰T​ϕ↔m⋅∇→​wm.\begin{split}\mathbf{w}^{T}\svec{\nabla}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}&=\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\mathbf{w}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}\right)-\nabla\mathbf{w}^{T}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}=\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\mathbf{w}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}\right)-\sum_{m=1}^{5}\mathbf{e}^{T}_{m}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}\cdot\svec{\nabla}w_{m}\\ &=\svec{\nabla}\cdot\svec{f}_{e}^{\mathcal{E}}-\sum_{m=1}^{5}\mathbf{w}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\phi}}_{m}\cdot\svec{\nabla}w_{m}.\end{split} (46)

Therefore,

𝐰T​(∇→⋅𝐟↔e​(𝐪)+∑m=15ϕ↔m​(𝐪)⋅∇→​wm)=∇→⋅f→eℰ.\mathbf{w}^{T}\left(\svec{\nabla}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}\left(\mathbf{q}\right)+\sum_{m=1}^{5}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{m}\left(\mathbf{q}\right)\cdot\svec{\nabla}w_{m}\right)=\svec{\nabla}\cdot\svec{f}_{e}^{\mathcal{E}}. (47)

The iNS/CH system does satisfy the property (44), for

𝐞1T​𝐟↔e=c​u→=𝐰T​ϕ↔1,𝐞2T​𝐟↔e=12​ρ​u​u→+p​e→1=𝐰T​ϕ↔2,𝐞3T​𝐟↔e=12​ρ​v​u→+p​e→2=𝐰T​ϕ↔3,𝐞4T​𝐟↔e=12​ρ​w​u→+p​e→3=𝐰T​ϕ↔4,𝐞5T​𝐟↔e=0=𝐰T​ϕ↔5.\begin{split}\mathbf{e}_{1}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}&=c\svec{u}=\mathbf{w}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{1},\\ \mathbf{e}_{2}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}&=\frac{1}{2}\rho u\svec{u}+p\svec{e}_{1}=\mathbf{w}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{2},\\ \mathbf{e}_{3}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}&=\frac{1}{2}\rho v\svec{u}+p\svec{e}_{2}=\mathbf{w}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{3},\\ \mathbf{e}_{4}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}&=\frac{1}{2}\rho w\svec{u}+p\svec{e}_{3}=\mathbf{w}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{4},\\ \mathbf{e}_{5}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}&=0=\mathbf{w}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{5}.\\ \end{split} (48)

So, the inviscid entropy flux for the iNS/CH system follows from (45) and is

f→eℰ=(12​ρ​vt​o​t2+p+μ​c)​u→.\svec{f}_{e}^{\mathcal{E}}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{tot}^{2}+p+\mu c\right)\svec{u}. (49)

For completeness, insight into how each of the different terms are combined into an entropy flux is provided in Appendix B.

Lastly, the entropy variables contract viscous fluxes. The entropy flux follows (45),

f→vℰ=𝐰T​𝐟↔v=M0​μ​∇→​μ+2​η​𝖲⋅u→.\svec{f}_{v}^{\mathcal{E}}=\mathbf{w}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{v}=M_{0}\mu\svec{\nabla}\mu+2\eta\mathsf{S}\cdot\svec{u}. (50)

Also, (36) holds,

∇→​𝐰T⋅𝐟↔v=M0​|∇→​μ|2+η⁡(∇→​u→+∇→​u→T):∇→​u→=M0​|∇→​μ|2+2​η​12​(∇→​u→+∇→​u→T):12​(∇→​u→+∇→​u→T)=M0​|∇→​μ|2+2​η​𝖲:𝖲⩾0.\begin{split}\svec{\nabla}\mathbf{w}^{T}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{v}&=M_{0}|\svec{\nabla}\mu|^{2}+\eta\left(\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}+\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}^{T}\right):\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}\\ &=M_{0}|\svec{\nabla}\mu|^{2}+2\eta\frac{1}{2}\left(\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}+\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}^{T}\right):\frac{1}{2}\left(\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}+\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}^{T}\right)\\ &=M_{0}|\svec{\nabla}\mu|^{2}+2\eta\mathsf{S}:\mathsf{S}\geqslant 0.\end{split} (51)

Therefore,

𝐰T​∇→⋅𝐟↔v=∇→⋅(𝐰T​𝐟↔v)−∇→​𝐰T⋅𝐟↔v⩽∇→⋅f→vℰ.\mathbf{w}^{T}\svec{\nabla}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{v}=\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\mathbf{w}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{v}\right)-\svec{\nabla}\mathbf{w}^{T}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{v}\leqslant\svec{\nabla}\cdot\svec{f}^{\mathcal{E}}_{v}. (52)

In (51), we replaced ∇→​u→\svec{\nabla}\svec{u} by its symmetric part (21) since it multiplies a symmetric tensor.

With these results, we confirm that the iNS/CH system, (20), with entropy, (37), satisfies the conservation law

ℰt+∇→⋅f→ℰ=−∇→𝐰T⋅𝐟↔v=−M0|∇→μ|2−2η𝖲:𝖲⩽0,\mathcal{E}_{t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\svec{f}^{\mathcal{E}}=-\svec{\nabla}\mathbf{w}^{T}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{v}=-M_{0}|\svec{\nabla}\mu|^{2}-2\eta\mathsf{S}:\mathsf{S}\leqslant 0, (53)

with entropy flux f→ℰ\svec{f}^{\mathcal{E}},

f→ℰ=f→tℰ+f→eℰ+f→vℰ=−32​σ​ε​ct​∇→​c+(12​ρ​vt​o​t2+p+μ​c)​u→+2​η​𝖲⋅u→+M0​μ​∇→​μ.\svec{f}^{\mathcal{E}}=\svec{f}^{\mathcal{E}}_{t}+\svec{f}^{\mathcal{E}}_{e}+\svec{f}^{\mathcal{E}}_{v}=-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon c_{t}\svec{\nabla}c+\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{tot}^{2}+p+\mu c\right)\svec{u}+2\eta\mathsf{S}\cdot\svec{u}+M_{0}\mu\svec{\nabla}\mu. (54)

Eq. (53) shows that the entropy (37) is always dissipated in the interior of the domain, and it can only increase due to boundary exchanges. The entropy equation can be written as a global equation by integrating over the whole domain Ω\Omega,

⁡d​ℰ¯⁡d​t+∫∂Ωf→ℰ⋅n→dS=−∫Ω(M0|∇→μ|2+2η𝖲:𝖲)dx→⩽0\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathcal{E}}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t}+\int_{\partial\Omega}\svec{f}^{\mathcal{E}}\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S=-\int_{\Omega}\left(M_{0}|\svec{\nabla}\mu|^{2}+2\eta\mathsf{S}:\mathsf{S}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\svec{x}\leqslant 0 (55)

where ℰ¯\bar{\mathcal{E}} is the total entropy,

ℰ¯=∫Ωℰ​⁡𝑑x→.\bar{\mathcal{E}}=\int_{\Omega}\mathcal{E}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\svec{x}. (56)

The discrete approximation will be constructed so that it mimics (55), which will guarantee that the discrete entropy of the approximation will remain bounded by the boundary and initial data.

2.1.1 Boundary conditions

Boundedness of the total entropy depends on proper specification of boundary conditions. We examine the effect of free– and no–slip boundary conditions. For the Cahn–Hilliard equation, we use a non–homogeneous Neumann condition for the concentration [33], and a homogeneous Neumann condition for the chemical potential,

−32​σ​ε​∂c∂n→|∂Ω=fw′​(c),∂μ∂n→|∂Ω=0,-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\frac{\partial c}{\partial\svec{n}}\biggr|_{\partial\Omega}=f_{w}^{\prime}(c),~~\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial\svec{n}}\biggr|_{\partial\Omega}=0, (57)

where fw​(c)f_{w}(c) is the boundary free–energy function that controls the wall contact angle. One choice is to use the function [33]

fw(c)=12σcosθw(2c−1)(1+2c−2c2),fw′(c)=6σcosθwc(1−c),f_{w}(c)=\frac{1}{2}\sigma\cos\theta_{w}(2c-1)(1+2c-2c^{2}),~~f_{w}^{\prime}(c)=6\sigma\cos\theta_{w}c(1-c), (58)

where θw\theta_{w} is the imposed contact angle with the wall. In most simulations performed in this work we use a 90∘90^{\circ} angle, which simplifies fw​(c)=0f_{w}(c)=0.

For free–slip boundary conditions, we impose zero normal velocity and zero normal stress for momentum, while for no–slip walls, all velocity components are zero (u→=0\svec{u}=0), and we do not impose any conditions on the stress tensor. Either way, the boundary entropy flux is,

f→ℰ⋅n→=−32σεct∇→c⋅n→+(12ρvt​o​t2+p+μc)u→⋅n→+2ηn→⋅𝖲⋅u→+M0μ∇→μ⋅n→.=ct​fw′​(c)=⁡d​fw⁡d​t,\begin{split}\svec{f}^{\mathcal{E}}\cdot\svec{n}&=-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon c_{t}\svec{\nabla}c\cdot\svec{n}+\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{tot}^{2}+p+\mu c\right)\svec{u}\cdot\svec{n}+2\eta\svec{n}\cdot\mathsf{S}\cdot\svec{u}+M_{0}\mu\svec{\nabla}\mu\cdot\svec{n}.\\ &=c_{t}f_{w}^{\prime}(c)=\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}f_{w}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t},\end{split} (59)

i.e., both entropy fluxes for the free– and no–slip walls coincide. The entropy balance (55) with wall boundary conditions is therefore

⁡d⁡d​t(ℰ¯+∫∂Ωfw(c)dS)=−∫Ω(M0|∇→μ|2+2η𝖲:𝖲)dx→⩽0,\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t}\left(\bar{\mathcal{E}}+\int_{\partial\Omega}f_{w}(c)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\right)=-\int_{\Omega}\left(M_{0}|\svec{\nabla}\mu|^{2}+2\eta\mathsf{S}:\mathsf{S}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\svec{x}\leqslant 0, (60)

where the volume entropy is augmented with the surface free energy as in [33, 8].

3 Space and time discretization

We now construct the entropy–stable DGSEM approximation. We restrict ourselves to the tensor product DGSEM with Gauss–Lobatto (GL) points, since it satisfies the Summation–By–Parts Simultaneous–Approximation–Term (SBP–SAT) property [11]. The SBP–SAT property allows us to discretely follow the continuous stability steps to construct a discrete entropy law.

3.1 Differential geometry and curvilinear elements

The physical domain Ω\Omega is tessellated with non–overlapping hexahedral elements, ee, which are geometrically transformed from a reference element E=[−1,1]3E=[-1,1]^{3}. This transformation is performed using a (polynomial) transfinite mapping X→\svec{X} that relates physical coordinates (x→=(x1,x2,x3)=(x,y,z)=x​x^+y​y^+z​z^\svec{x}=\left(x^{1},x^{2},x^{3}\right)=\left(x,y,z\right)=x\hat{x}+y\hat{y}+z\hat{z}) to local reference coordinates (ξ→=(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=(ξ,η,ζ)=ξ​ξ^+η​η^+ζ​ζ^\svec{\xi}=\left(\xi^{1},\xi^{2},\xi^{3}\right)=\left(\xi,\eta,\zeta\right)=\xi\hat{\xi}+\eta\hat{\eta}+\zeta\hat{\zeta}) through

x→=X→​(ξ→)=X→​(ξ,η,ζ).\svec{x}=\svec{X}\left(\svec{\xi}\right)=\svec{X}\left(\xi,\eta,\zeta\right). (61)

The space vectors x^i\hat{x}_{i} and ξ^i\hat{\xi}^{i} are unit vectors in the three Cartesian directions of physical and reference coordinates, respectively.

From the transformation (61) one can define three covariant basis vectors,

a→i=∂X→∂ξi,i=1,2,3,\svec{a}_{i}=\frac{\partial\svec{X}}{\partial\xi^{i}},~~i=1,2,3, (62)

and three contravariant basis vectors,

a→i=∇→​ξi=1J​(a→j×a→k),(i,j,k)​ cyclic,\svec{a}^{i}=\svec{\nabla}\xi^{i}=\frac{1}{J}\left(\svec{a}_{j}\times\svec{a}_{k}\right),~~(i,j,k)\text{ cyclic}, (63)

where

J=a→1⋅(a→2×a→3)J=\svec{a}_{1}\cdot\left(\svec{a}_{2}\times\svec{a}_{3}\right) (64)

is the Jacobian of the mapping X→\svec{X}. The contravariant coordinate vectors satisfy the metric identities [34],

∑i=13∂(J​ani)∂ξi=0,n=1,2,3,\sum_{i=1}^{3}\frac{\partial\left(Ja_{n}^{i}\right)}{\partial\xi^{i}}=0,~~n=1,2,3, (65)

where ania_{n}^{i} is the nn–th Cartesian component of the contravariant vector a→i\svec{a}^{i}.

We use the volume weighted contravariant basis J​a→iJ\svec{a}^{i} to transform differential operators from physical (∇→\svec{\nabla}) to reference (∇→ξ\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}) space. The divergence of a vector is [16]

∇→⋅f→=1J​∇→ξ⋅(𝖬T​f→),\svec{\nabla}\cdot\svec{f}=\frac{1}{J}\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\cdot\left(\mathsf{M}^{T}\svec{f}\right), (66)

where 𝖬=(J​a→ξ,J​a→η,J​a→ζ)\mathsf{M}=\left(J\svec{a}^{\xi},J\svec{a}^{\eta},J\svec{a}^{\zeta}\right). We use (28) to write the divergence of an entire block vector compactly. Thus, we define the block matrix ℳ\mathcal{M},

ℳ=(J​a11​𝐈¯5J​a12​𝐈¯5J​a13​𝐈¯5J​a21​𝐈¯5J​a22​𝐈¯5J​a23​𝐈¯5J​a31​𝐈¯5J​a32​𝐈¯5J​a33​𝐈¯5),\mathcal{M}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}Ja^{1}_{1}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}&Ja^{2}_{1}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}&Ja^{3}_{1}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}\\ Ja^{1}_{2}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}&Ja^{2}_{2}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}&Ja^{3}_{2}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}\\ Ja^{1}_{3}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}&Ja^{2}_{3}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}&Ja^{3}_{3}\underline{\mathbf{I}}_{5}\end{array}\right), (67)

which allows us to write (66) for all the state variables simultaneously,

∇→⋅𝐟↔=1J​∇→ξ⋅(ℳT​𝐟↔)=1J​∇→ξ⋅𝐟~↔,\svec{\nabla}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}=\frac{1}{J}\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\cdot\left(\mathcal{M}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}\right)=\frac{1}{J}\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}}, (68)

with 𝐟~↔\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}} being the block vector of the contravariant fluxes,

𝐟~↔=ℳT​𝐟↔,𝐟~i=J​a→i⋅𝐟↔.\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}}=\mathcal{M}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}},~~\tilde{\mathbf{f}}^{i}=J\svec{a}^{i}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}. (69)

The gradient of a scalar is [16]

∇→​w=1J​𝖬​∇→ξ​w,\svec{\nabla}w=\frac{1}{J}\mathsf{M}\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}w, (70)

which we can also extend to all entropy variables using (67),

𝐠↔=∇→​𝐰=1J​ℳ​∇→ξ​𝐰,\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{g}}=\svec{\nabla}\mathbf{w}=\frac{1}{J}{\mathcal{M}}\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\mathbf{w}, (71)

and to non–conservative terms,

ϕ↔m⋅∇→​wm=1𝒥​ϕ~↔m⋅∇→ξ​wm.\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{m}\cdot\svec{\nabla}w_{m}=\frac{1}{\mathcal{J}}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}_{m}\cdot\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}w_{m}. (72)

To transform the iNS/CH system, (20), into reference space, we first write it as a first order system. To do so, we define the auxiliary variables 𝐠↔=∇→​𝐰\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{g}}=\svec{\nabla}\mathbf{w} and g→c=∇→​c\svec{g}_{c}=\svec{\nabla}c so that

𝐦¯​𝐪t+∇→⋅𝐟↔e​(𝐪)+∑m=15(ϕ↔m​(𝐪)⋅∇→​wm)=∇→⋅𝐟↔v​(𝐠↔)+𝐬⁡(𝐪),𝐠↔=∇→​𝐰,μ=f0′​(c)−32​σ​ε​∇→⋅g→c,g→c=∇→​c.\begin{split}&\underline{\mathbf{m}}\mathbf{q}_{t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}(\mathbf{q})+\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{m}\left(\mathbf{q}\right)\cdot\svec{\nabla}w_{m}\right)=\svec{\nabla}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{v}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{g}}\right)+\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{q}),\\ &\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{g}}=\svec{\nabla}\mathbf{w},\\ &\mu=f_{0}^{\prime}(c)-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\svec{\nabla}\cdot\svec{g}_{c},\\ &\svec{g}_{c}=\svec{\nabla}c.\end{split} (73)

Recall that the viscous fluxes of the incompressible NSE depend only on the gradient of the entropy variables, 𝐠↔\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{g}}, and not on the state vector 𝐪\mathbf{q}. Note that in the first equation the non–conservative terms are written in terms of ∇→​𝐰\svec{\nabla}\mathbf{w} and not in terms of 𝐠↔\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{g}}. This allows us to construct an entropy–stable scheme.

Next, we transform the operators to reference space using (68), (71), and (72)

J​𝐦¯​𝐪t+∇→ξ⋅𝐟~↔e​(𝐪)+∑m=15(ϕ~↔m​(𝐪)⋅∇→ξ​wm)=∇→ξ⋅𝐟~↔v​(𝐠↔)+J​𝐬​(𝐪),\displaystyle J\underline{\mathbf{m}}\mathbf{q}_{t}+\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}}_{e}(\mathbf{q})+\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}_{m}\left(\mathbf{q}\right)\cdot\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}w_{m}\right)=\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}}_{v}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{g}}\right)+J\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{q}), (74a)
J​𝐠↔=ℳ​∇→ξ​𝐰,\displaystyle J\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{g}}={\mathcal{M}}\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\mathbf{w}, (74b)
J​μ=J​f0′​(c)−32​σ​ε​∇→ξ⋅g~→c,\displaystyle J\mu=Jf_{0}^{\prime}(c)-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\cdot\svec{\tilde{g}}_{c}, (74c)
J​g→c=𝖬​∇→ξ​c,\displaystyle J\svec{g}_{c}=\mathsf{M}\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}c, (74d)

to obtain the final form of the equations to be approximated.

The DG approximation is obtained from weak forms of the equations (74). We first define the inner product in the reference element, EE, for state and block vectors

⟨𝐟,𝐠⟩E=∫E𝐟T𝐠dE,⟨𝐟↔,𝐠↔⟩E=∫E𝐟↔⋅𝐠↔dE.\left\langle\mathbf{f},\mathbf{g}\right\rangle_{E}=\int_{E}\mathbf{f}^{T}\mathbf{g}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}E,~~\left\langle\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}},\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{g}}\right\rangle_{E}=\int_{E}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{g}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}E. (75)

We construct four weak forms by multiplying (74) by four test functions 𝝋q\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{q}, 𝝋↔g\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\varphi}}_{g}, φμ{\varphi}_{\mu}, and φ→c\svec{\varphi}_{c}, then we integrate over the reference element EE, and finally we integrate by parts to get

J\underline{\mathbf{m}}\mathbf{q}_{t},\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{q}\right\rangle_{E}&+\int_{\partial E}\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{q}^{T}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}}_{e}+\sum_{m=1}^{5}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}_{m}w_{m}-\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}}_{v}\right)\cdot\hat{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S_{\xi}-\left\langle\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}}_{e},\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{q}\right\rangle_{E}\\ &-\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left\langle J\mathbf{s},\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{q}\right\rangle_{E},\\ \left\langle E}\mathbf{w}^{T}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\varphi}}}_{g}\cdot\hat{n}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S_{\xi}-\left\langle\mathbf{w},\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\varphi}}}_{g}\right\rangle_{E},\\ \left\langle J\mu,\varphi_{\mu}\right\rangle_{E}&=\left\langle Jf_{0}^{\prime},\varphi_{\mu}\right\rangle_{E}-\int_{\partial E}\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\varphi_{\mu}\svec{\tilde{g}}_{c}\cdot\hat{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S_{\xi}+\left\langle\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\svec{\tilde{g}}_{c},\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\varphi_{\mu}\right\rangle_{E},\\ \left\langle J\svec{g}_{c},\svec{\varphi}_{c}\right\rangle_{E}&=\int_{\partial E}c\svec{\tilde{\varphi}}_{c}\cdot\hat{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S_{\xi}-\left\langle c,\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\cdot\svec{\tilde{\varphi}}_{c}\right\rangle_{E}.\end{split} (76)

The quantities n^\hat{n} and ⁡d​Sξ\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S_{\xi} are the unit outward pointing normal and surface differential at the faces of EE, respectively. The contravariant test functions 𝝋~↔g\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\varphi}}}_{g} and φ~→c\svec{\tilde{\varphi}}_{c} follow the definition (69). Finally, surface integrals extend to all six faces of an element,

∫∂Ef~→⋅n^dSξ=∫[−1,1]2f~1dηdζ|ξ=−1ξ=1+∫[−1,1]2f~2dξdζ|η=−1η=1+∫[−1,1]2f~3dξdη|ζ=−1ζ=1.\int_{\partial E}\svec{\tilde{f}}\cdot\hat{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S_{\xi}=\int_{[-1,1]^{2}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\tilde{f}^{1}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\eta\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\zeta\biggr|_{\xi=-1}^{\xi=1}\!\!+\int_{[-1,1]^{2}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\tilde{f}^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\zeta\biggr|_{\eta=-1}^{\eta=1}\!\!+\int_{[-1,1]^{2}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\tilde{f}^{3}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\eta\biggr|_{\zeta=-1}^{\zeta=1}. (77)

We can write surface integrals in either physical or reference space. The relation between physical and reference surface differentials is given by,

⁡d​Si=|J​a→i|​⁡d​ξj​⁡d​ξk=𝒥fi​⁡d​Sξi,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S^{i}=\left|J\svec{a}^{i}\right|\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi^{j}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi^{k}=\mathcal{J}_{f}^{i}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S_{\xi}^{i}, (78)

where we have defined the face Jacobian 𝒥fi=|𝒥​a→i|\mathcal{J}_{f}^{i}=\left|\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{i}\right|. We can write the surface flux in either reference element, f~→⋅n^\svec{\tilde{f}}\cdot\hat{{n}}, or physical, f→⋅n→\svec{f}\cdot\svec{n}, variables through

f~→⋅n^idSξ=(𝓜Tf→)⋅n^idSξ=f→⋅(𝓜n^i)dSξ=f→⋅n→|Ja→i|dSξ=f→⋅n→idS.{\svec{\tilde{f}}}\cdot\hat{{n}}^{i}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S_{\xi}=\left(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}^{T}\svec{f}\right)\cdot\hat{{n}}^{i}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S_{\xi}=\svec{f}\cdot\left(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}\hat{{n}}^{i}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S_{\xi}=\svec{f}\cdot\svec{n}\left|J\svec{a}^{i}\right|\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S_{\xi}=\svec{f}\cdot\svec{n}^{i}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S. (79)

Therefore, the surface integrals can be written in both physical and reference spaces,

∫∂Ef→~⋅𝐧^dSξ=∫∂ef→⋅n→dS,\int_{\partial E}\tilde{\svec{f}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S_{\xi}=\int_{\partial e}\svec{f}\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S, (80)

and we will use one or the other depending on whether we are studying an isolated element (reference space) or the entire mesh (physical space).

3.2 Polynomial approximation and the DGSEM

We now construct the discrete version of (76). The approximation of the state vector inside each element EE is an order NN polynomial,

𝐪≈𝐐⁡(ξ→)=∑i,j,k=0N𝐐i​j​k​(t)​li​(ξ)​lj​(η)​lk​(ζ)∈ℙN,\mathbf{q}\approx\mathbf{Q}\left(\svec{\xi}\right)=\sum_{i,j,k=0}^{N}\mathbf{Q}_{ijk}(t)l_{i}(\xi)l_{j}(\eta)l_{k}(\zeta)\in\mathbb{P}^{N}, (81)

where ℙN\mathbb{P}^{N} is the space of polynomials of degree less than or equal to NN on [−1,1]3[-1,1]^{3}. The state values 𝐐i​j​k​(t)=𝐐⁡(ξi,ηj,ζk,t)\mathbf{Q}_{ijk}(t)=\mathbf{Q}(\xi_{i},\eta_{j},\zeta_{k},t) are the nodal degrees of freedom (time dependent coefficients) at the tensor product of each of the Gauss–Lobatto (GL) points {ξi}i=0N\{\xi_{i}\}_{i=0}^{N}. Then, Lagrange polynomials li​(ξ)l_{i}(\xi) are

li​(ξ)=∏j=0j≠iNξ−ξjξi−ξj.l_{i}(\xi)=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=0\\ j\neq i\end{subarray}}^{N}\frac{\xi-\xi_{j}}{\xi_{i}-\xi_{j}}. (82)

The geometry and metric terms are also approximated with order N polynomials. Let us denote 𝕀N\mathbb{I}^{N} as the polynomial interpolation operator [35]. The transfinite mapping is approximated using 𝒳=𝕀N​(X)\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{I}^{N}\left(X\right), but special attention must be paid to its derivatives (i.e. the contravariant basis) since 𝒥​a→i≠𝕀N​(a→j×a→k)\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{i}\neq\mathbb{I}^{N}\left(\svec{a}_{j}\times\svec{a}_{k}\right). For the metric identities (65) to hold discretely,

∑i=13∂𝕀N​(J​ani)∂ξi=0,n=1,2,3,\sum_{i=1}^{3}\frac{\partial\mathbb{I}^{N}\left(Ja_{n}^{i}\right)}{\partial\xi^{i}}=0,~~n=1,2,3, (83)

we approximate metric terms using the curl form [34],

𝒥ani=−x^i⋅∇→ξ×(𝕀N(𝒳l∇→ξ𝒳m))∈ℙN,i=1,2,3,n=1,2,3,(n,m,l) cyclic.\mathcal{J}a_{n}^{i}=-\hat{x}_{i}\cdot\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\times\left(\mathbb{I}^{N}\left(\mathcal{X}_{l}\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\mathcal{X}_{m}\right)\right)\in\mathbb{P}^{N},~~~i=1,2,3,~~n=1,2,3,~~(n,m,l)\text{ cyclic}. (84)

If we compute 𝒥​a→i\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{i} using (84), we ensure discrete free–stream preservation, which is crucial to avoid grid induced solution changes [34].

Next, we approximate integrals that arise in the weak formulation using Gauss quadratures. Let {wi}i=0N\{w_{i}\}_{i=0}^{N} be the quadrature weights associated to Gauss–Lobatto nodes {ξi}i=0N\{\xi_{i}\}_{i=0}^{N}. Then, in one dimension,

∫−11f⁡(ξ)​⁡𝑑ξ≈∫Nf⁡(ξ)​⁡𝑑ξ=∑m=0Nwm​f​(ξm)=∑m=0Nwm​Fm.\int_{-1}^{1}f(\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi\approx\int_{N}f(\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi=\sum_{m=0}^{N}w_{m}f(\xi_{m})=\sum_{m=0}^{N}w_{m}F_{m}. (85)

For Gauss–Lobatto points, the approximation is exact if f⁡(ξ)∈ℙ2​N−1f\left(\xi\right)\in\mathbb{P}^{2N-1}. The extension to three dimensions has three nested quadratures, one for each of the three reference space dimensions. For example, the inner product is

⟨f,g⟩E≈⟨f,g⟩E,N=∑m,n,l=0Nwm​n​l​Fm​n​l​Gm​n​l,wm​n​l=wm​wn​wl,\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{E}\approx\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{E,N}=\sum_{m,n,l=0}^{N}w_{mnl}F_{mnl}G_{mnl},~~w_{mnl}=w_{m}w_{n}w_{l}, (86)

with a similar definition for block vectors. The approximation of surface integrals is performed similarly, replacing exact integrals by Gauss quadratures in (77),

Gauss–Lobatto points are used to construct entropy–stable schemes using split–forms [11, 18]. There is no need to perform an interpolation from the volume polynomials in (87) to the boundaries, since boundary points are included, which is known as the Simultaneous–Approximation–Term (SAT) property. The exactness of the numerical quadrature and the SAT property yield the discrete Gauss law [11, 36]: for any polynomials 𝐅↔\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}} and 𝐕\mathbf{V} in ℙN\mathbb{P}^{N},

In (89), the test functions are restricted to polynomial spaces, ℙN\mathbb{P}^{N}. Taken in context, μ\mu (which lacks an upper case symbol) refers to the polynomial approximation of the chemical potential.

Euler conservative fluxes and viscous fluxes have inter–element coupling and physical boundary conditions enforced by numerical fluxes in the element boundary quadratures in (89),

Both numerical and diamond flux functions are detailed below in Sec. 3.3. In (90) and (91), LL and RR represent the values from the left and right adjacent elements. Although numerical fluxes are single valued at each interface, diamond fluxes are not so constrained and their value can jump from one side to the other.

The algorithm efficiency is improved by the use of single calculation of the local gradient of the entropy variables, ∇→ξ​𝐖\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\mathbf{W}, for both non–conservative terms in (93a) and gradients in (93b). As a result, non–conservative terms are as expensive as source terms (i.e. no additional matrix multiplications are required). Then for the gradients 𝐆↔\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{G}} we augment the pre–computed local gradients ∇→ξ​𝐖\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\mathbf{W} with the surface integral in (93b).

The point–wise discretization is obtained by replacing the test function in (93) by the Lagrange polynomials. For completeness, we write the implementation of the discretization in Appendix C.

3.3 Numerical fluxes

The approximation (93) is completed with the specification of numerical fluxes 𝐅e⋆{\mathbf{F}}_{e}^{\star}, 𝐅v⋆{\mathbf{F}}_{v}^{\star}, 𝐖⋆\mathbf{W}^{\star}, G→c⋆\svec{G}_{c}^{\star}, C⋆C^{\star}, and diamond fluxes (𝚽↔m​Wm)♢(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m})^{\diamondsuit}. For the inviscid fluxes we propose two options: an entropy conserving option using using central fluxes, and an entropy–stable approximation using the exact Riemann solver derived in [25]. For the viscous fluxes and concentration gradient, we use the Bassi–Rebay 1 (BR1) scheme [38].

Before we write the numerical fluxes, we first describe the rotational invariance property satisfied by inviscid fluxes and non–conservative terms. The rotational invariance of the flux [39] allows us to write the normal flux 𝐅↔e⋅n→\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}\cdot\svec{n} from a rotated version of the inviscid flux xx–component 𝐅e\mathbf{F}_{e},

𝐅↔e⋅n→=𝐓¯T​𝐅e​(𝐓¯​𝐐)=𝐓¯T​𝐅e​(𝐐n),𝐓¯=(100000nxnynz00t1,xt1,yt1,z00t2,xt2,yt2,z000001),\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}\cdot\svec{n}=\underline{\mathbf{T}}^{T}\mathbf{F}_{e}\left(\underline{\mathbf{T}}\mathbf{Q}\right)=\underline{\mathbf{T}}^{T}\mathbf{F}_{e}\left(\mathbf{Q}_{n}\right),~~\underline{\mathbf{T}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}1&0&0&0&0\\ 0&n_{x}&n_{y}&n_{z}&0\\ 0&t_{1,x}&t_{1,y}&t_{1,z}&0\\ 0&t_{2,x}&t_{2,y}&t_{2,z}&0\\ 0&0&0&0&1\end{array}\right), (94)

where 𝐓¯\underline{\mathbf{T}} is a rotation matrix that only affects velocities, n→=(nx,ny,nz)\svec{n}=\left(n_{x},n_{y},n_{z}\right) is the normal unit vector to the face, and t→1\svec{t}_{1} and t→2\svec{t}_{2} are two tangent unit vectors to the face. When the rotation matrix 𝐓¯\underline{\mathbf{T}} multiplies the state vector 𝐐\mathbf{Q}, we obtain the face normal state vector 𝐐n\mathbf{Q}_{n},

𝐐n=𝐓¯​𝐐=(C,ρ​Un,ρ​Vt​1,ρ​Vt​2,P),\mathbf{Q}_{n}=\underline{\mathbf{T}}\mathbf{Q}=\left(C,\sqrt{\rho}U_{n},\sqrt{\rho}V_{t1},\sqrt{\rho}V_{t2},P\right), (95)

where Un=U→⋅n→U_{n}=\svec{U}\cdot\svec{n} the normal velocity, and Vt​i=U→⋅t→iV_{ti}=\svec{U}\cdot\svec{t}_{i} (i=1,2i=1,2) are the two tangent velocities. Note that the reference system rotation does not affect the total speed

Vt​o​t2=U2+V2+W2=Un2+Vt​12+Vt​22.V_{tot}^{2}=U^{2}+V^{2}+W^{2}=U_{n}^{2}+V_{t1}^{2}+V_{t2}^{2}. (96)

The non–conservative terms,

3.3.1 Inviscid fluxes: entropy conserving central fluxes

The first choice for the inviscid numerical and diamond fluxes is to use central fluxes, which will lead to an entropy conserving approximation. We adapt the approach used for the resistive MHD in [37], so that

𝐅↔e⋆⋅n→={{𝐅↔e}}⋅n→=𝐓¯T​({{C​Un}}{{12​ρ​Un2+p}}{{12​ρ​Un​Vt​1}}{{12​ρ​Un​Vt​2}}0),\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}^{\star}\cdot\svec{n}=\{\!\{\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}\}\!\}\cdot\svec{n}=\underline{\mathbf{T}}^{T}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\{\!\{CU_{n}\}\!\}\\ \{\!\{\frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}^{2}+p\}\!\}\\ \{\!\{\frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}V_{t1}\}\!\}\\ \{\!\{\frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}V_{t2}\}\!\}\\ 0\end{array}\right), (100)

and

∑m=15(𝚽↔m​Wm)♢⋅n→=∑m=15𝚽↔m​{{Wm}}⋅n→=𝐓¯T​(012​ρ​Un​{{Un}}+C⁡{{μ}}12​ρ​Un​{{Vt​1}}12​ρ​Un​{{Vt​2}}ρ0​c02​{{Un}}).\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right)^{\diamondsuit}\cdot\svec{n}=\sum_{m=1}^{5}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}\{\!\{W_{m}\}\!\}\cdot\svec{n}=\underline{\mathbf{T}}^{T}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}\{\!\{U_{n}\}\!\}+C\{\!\{\mu\}\!\}\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}\{\!\{V_{t1}\}\!\}\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}\{\!\{V_{t2}\}\!\}\\ \rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}\{\!\{U_{n}\}\!\}\end{array}\right). (101)

In (100) and (101), {{u}}\{\!\{u\}\!\} represents the average operator,

{{u}}=uL+uR2\{\!\{u\}\!\}=\frac{u_{L}+u_{R}}{2} (102)

and 𝚽↔m\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m} (without average) represents the element local state at the face.

3.3.2 Inviscid fluxes: entropy–stable exact Riemann solver (ERS)

The second option uses the solution of the exact Riemann problem derived in [25]. The star region solution of the incompressible NSE (i.e. without the Cahn–Hilliard equation) is,

Un⋆=PL−PR+ρL​Un​L​λL+−ρR​Un​R​λR−ρL​λL+−ρR​λR−,P⋆=PL+ρLλ+L(Un​L−Un⋆),ρ⋆={ρL⋆ if Un⋆⩾0ρR⋆ if Un⋆<0,ρL⋆=ρL​λL+Un⋆−λL−,ρR⋆=ρR​λR−Un⋆−λR+,Vt​i⋆={Vt​i​L if Un⋆⩾0Vt​i​R if Un⋆<0,\begin{split}U_{n}^{\star}&=\frac{P_{L}-P_{R}+\rho_{L}U_{nL}\lambda_{L}^{+}-\rho_{R}U_{nR}\lambda_{R}^{-}}{\rho_{L}\lambda_{L}^{+}-\rho_{R}\lambda_{R}^{-}},~~P^{\star}=P_{L}+\rho_{L}\lambda^{+}_{L}\left(U_{nL}-U_{n}^{\star}\right),\\ \rho^{\star}&=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}\rho_{L}^{\star}&\text{ if }&U_{n}^{\star}\geqslant 0\\ \rho_{R}^{\star}&\text{ if }&U_{n}^{\star}<0\end{array}\right.,~~\rho_{L}^{\star}=\frac{\rho_{L}\lambda_{L}^{+}}{U_{n}^{\star}-\lambda_{L}^{-}},~~\rho_{R}^{\star}=\frac{\rho_{R}\lambda_{R}^{-}}{U_{n}^{\star}-\lambda_{R}^{+}},~~V_{ti}^{\star}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}V_{tiL}&\text{ if }&U_{n}^{\star}\geqslant 0\\ V_{tiR}&\text{ if }&U_{n}^{\star}<0\end{array}\right.,\end{split} (103)

with eigenvalues,

λL±=Un​L±aL2,λR±=Un​R±aR2,a=Un2+4​ρ0​c02ρ.\lambda_{L}^{\pm}=\frac{U_{nL}\pm a_{L}}{2},~~\lambda_{R}^{\pm}=\frac{U_{nR}\pm a_{R}}{2},~~a=\sqrt{U_{n}^{2}+\frac{4\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}}{\rho}}. (104)

We evaluate the numerical flux with the star region solution with the normal state 𝐐n\mathbf{Q}_{n} in (94) for the momentum, and perform the average for the Cahn-Hilliard part,

𝐅↔e⋆⋅n→=𝐓¯T​({{C​Un}}12​ρ⋆​Un⋆,2+p⋆12​ρ⋆​Un⋆​Vt​1⋆12​ρ⋆​Un⋆​Vt​2⋆0).\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}^{\star}\cdot\svec{n}=\underline{\mathbf{T}}^{T}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\{\!\{CU_{n}\}\!\}\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star,2}+p^{\star}\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}V_{t1}^{\star}\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}V_{t2}^{\star}\\ 0\end{array}\right). For non–conservative terms, we choose the diamond fluxes,

∑m=15(𝚽↔m​Wm)♢⋅n→=𝚽↔1​{{W1}}⋅n→+∑m=25(𝚽↔m⋆​Wm⋆+𝚽↔m​Wm−𝚽↔m⋆​Wm)⋅n→=𝐓¯T​(012​ρ⋆​Un⋆,2+12​ρ​Un2−12​ρ⋆​Un⋆​Un+C⁡{{μ}}12​ρ⋆​Un⋆​Vt​1⋆+12​ρ​Un​Vt​1−12​ρ⋆​Un⋆​Vt​112​ρ⋆​Un⋆​Vt​2⋆+12​ρ​Un​Vt​2−12​ρ⋆​Un⋆​Vt​2ρ0​c02​Un⋆)=𝐓¯T​𝐅Φ​WERS,\begin{split}\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right)^{\diamondsuit}\cdot\svec{n}&=\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{1}\{\!\{W_{1}\}\!\}\cdot\svec{n}+\sum_{m=2}^{5}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}^{\star}W^{\star}_{m}+\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}-\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}^{\star}W_{m}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\\ &=\underline{\mathbf{T}}^{T}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star,2}+\frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}U_{n}+C\{\!\{\mu\}\!\}\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}V_{t1}^{\star}+\frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}V_{t1}-\frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}V_{t1}\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}V_{t2}^{\star}+\frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}V_{t2}-\frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}V_{t2}\\ \rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}U_{n}^{\star}\end{array}\right)=\underline{\mathbf{T}}^{T}\mathbf{F}_{\Phi W}^{\mathrm{ERS}},\end{split} (106)

where 𝚽↔m⋆\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}^{\star} and Wm⋆W_{m}^{\star} refer to non–conservative coefficients and entropy variables evaluated with the star region solution (103). This choice is justified by the stability analysis.

3.3.3 Viscous and chemical potential fluxes: Bassi–Rebay 1 (BR1) method

For the viscous fluxes and the chemical potential we use the Bassi–Rebay 1 (BR1) scheme [38], which averages entropy variables and fluxes between the adjacent elements. However, for the Cahn–Hilliard equation, we include the possibility to add interface stabilization. Although it is not a requirement for stability, we have found it enhances accuracy when the flow configuration is under–resolved [8]. The viscous and Cahn–Hilliard fluxes are,

𝐖⋆={{𝐖}},𝐅↔v⋆={{𝐅↔v}}+β⁡⟦μ⟧​𝐞1​n→L,C⋆={{C}},G→c⋆={{G→c}}+β⁡⟦C⟧​n→L,\mathbf{W}^{\star}=\{\!\{\mathbf{W}\}\!\},~~{\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}}_{v}^{\star}=\{\!\{{\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}}_{v}\}\!\}+\beta\left\llbracket\mu\right\rrbracket\mathbf{e}_{1}\svec{n}_{L},~~C^{\star}=\{\!\{C\}\!\},~~\svec{G}_{c}^{\star}=\{\!\{\svec{G}_{c}\}\!\}+\beta\left\llbracket C\right\rrbracket\svec{n}_{L}, (107)

where β\beta is the penalty parameter, computed in this work following [40, 8],

β=κβ​N⁡(N+1)2​|𝒥f|​{{𝒥−1}},\beta=\kappa_{\beta}\frac{N(N+1)}{2}|\mathcal{J}_{f}|\{\!\{\mathcal{J}^{-1}\}\!\}, (108)

with κβ\kappa_{\beta} a dimensionless free parameter (in this work we only use κβ=0\kappa_{\beta}=0 to disable interface stabilization, and κβ=1\kappa_{\beta}=1 to enable interface stabilization), we define the inter–element jumps as ⟦∙⟧=∙R−∙L\left\llbracket\bullet\right\rrbracket=\bullet_{R}-\bullet_{L}, and n→L\svec{n}_{L} is the outward normal vector to the left element. In (108) NN is the polynomial order, |𝒥f||\mathcal{J}_{f}| is the surface Jacobian of the face, and {{𝒥−1}}\{\!\{\mathcal{J}^{-1}\}\!\} is the average of the inverse of the Jacobians of left and right elements.

3.4 Boundary conditions

The approximation is completed with the addition of boundary conditions. Here we show how we impose free– and no–slip wall boundary conditions. The boundary conditions are imposed through the numerical and diamond fluxes at the physical boundary faces. We consider the inviscid and viscous fluxes individually.

3.4.1 Inviscid flux

The inviscid numerical flux controls the normal velocity u→⋅n→=0\svec{u}\cdot\svec{n}=0 for both free– and no–slip boundary conditions. Again, as at interior faces, we provide an entropy conserving option with central fluxes, and an entropy stable version with the exact Riemann problem solution. Either way, we apply central fluxes (100)–(101) or the ERS (105)–(106) to the interior state 𝐐ni\mathbf{Q}_{n}^{i} and a mirrored ghost state 𝐐ne\mathbf{Q}_{n}^{e},

𝐐ni=(Cρ​Unρ​Vt​1ρ​Vt​2P),𝐐ne=(C−ρ​Unρ​Vt​1ρ​Vt​2P).\mathbf{Q}_{n}^{i}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}C\\ \sqrt{\rho}U_{n}\\ \sqrt{\rho}V_{t1}\\ \sqrt{\rho}V_{t2}\\ P\end{array}\right),~~\mathbf{Q}_{n}^{e}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}C\\ -\sqrt{\rho}U_{n}\\ \sqrt{\rho}V_{t1}\\ \sqrt{\rho}V_{t2}\\ P\end{array}\right). (109)

The fluxes differ depending on which numerical flux is used.

  1. 1.

    The entropy conserving approximation with central fluxes. The numerical (100) and diamond (101) central fluxes for (109) are,

    𝐅↔e⋆⋅n→=𝐓¯T​(012​ρ​Un2+P000),∑m=15(𝚽↔m​Wm)♢⋅n→=𝐓¯T​(0C​μ12​ρ​Un​Vt​112​ρ​Un​Vt​20).\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}^{\star}\cdot\svec{n}=\underline{\mathbf{T}}^{T}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}^{2}+P\\ 0\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right),~~\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right)^{\diamondsuit}\cdot\svec{n}=\underline{\mathbf{T}}^{T}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ C\mu\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}V_{t1}\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}V_{t2}\\ 0\end{array}\right). (110)
  2. 2.

    The entropy stable approximation with the exact Riemann solver. The star region values computed from the states (109) are

    Un⋆=0,P⋆=P+ρ​λ+​Un,λ+=Un+a2.U_{n}^{\star}=0,~~P^{\star}=P+\rho\lambda^{+}U_{n},~~\lambda^{+}=\frac{U_{n}+a}{2}. (111)

    With these star values the numerical (105) and diamond (106) fluxes become

    𝐅↔e⋆⋅n→=𝐓¯T​(0P+ρ​λ+​Un000),∑m=15(𝚽↔m​Wm)♢⋅n→=𝐓¯T​(012​ρ​Un2+C​μ12​ρ​Un​Vt​112​ρ​Un​Vt​20).\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}^{\star}\cdot\svec{n}=\underline{\mathbf{T}}^{T}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ P+\rho\lambda^{+}U_{n}\\ 0\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right),~~\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right)^{\diamondsuit}\cdot\svec{n}=\underline{\mathbf{T}}^{T}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}^{2}+C\mu\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}V_{t1}\\ \frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}V_{t2}\\ 0\end{array}\right). (112)

3.4.2 Viscous and Cahn–Hilliard fluxes

For the free–slip wall boundary condition, we impose zero normal stress 𝖲⋅n→=0\mathsf{S}\cdot\svec{n}=0 (Neumann), whereas for the no–slip wall boundary condition, we impose zero velocity u→=0\svec{u}=0 (Dirichlet). Furthermore, we implement the discrete version of the homogeneous and non–homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions (57) for the Cahn–Hilliard equation. The concentration, concentration gradient, entropy variables, and viscous fluxes at the boundaries are:

  1. 1.

    Free–slip wall boundary condition.

    C⋆=C,G→c⋆=g′​(C),𝐖⋆=𝐖,𝐅↔v⋆⋅n→=0.C^{\star}=C,~~\svec{G}_{c}^{\star}=g^{\prime}(C),~~\mathbf{W}^{\star}=\mathbf{W},~~\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}^{\star}_{v}\cdot\svec{n}=0. (113)
  2. 2.

    No–slip wall boundary condition.

    C⋆=C,G→c⋆=g′​(C),𝐖⋆=(μ,0,0,0,P),𝐅↔v⋆⋅n→=(02​η​𝒮0)⋅n→.C^{\star}=C,~~\svec{G}_{c}^{\star}=g^{\prime}(C),~~\mathbf{W}^{\star}=\left(\mu,0,0,0,P\right),~~\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}^{\star}\cdot\svec{n}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ 2\eta\mathcal{S}\\ 0\end{array}\right)\cdot\svec{n}. (114)

3.5 Implicit–Explicit (IMEX) time discretization

The fully–discrete scheme is completed with the discretization of the time derivatives 𝐐t\mathbf{Q}_{t} in (93). The numerical stiffness induced by the fourth order derivatives present in the Cahn–Hilliard equation prevents us from practically using fully explicit time marching. Therefore, we use the IMplicit–EXplicit (IMEX) Backward Differentiation Formula (BDF) time integrator described in [24]. We revisit the continuous setting (20)

ct+∇→⋅(c​u→)=M0​∇→2​(f0′​(c)−32​σ​ε​∇→2​c),ρ​(ρ​u→)t+∇→⋅(12​ρ​u→​u→)+12​ρ​u→⋅∇→​u→+c​∇→​μ=−∇→​p+2​η​𝖲+ρ​g→,pt+ρ0​c02​∇→⋅u→=0,\begin{split}&c_{t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(c\svec{u}\right)=M_{0}\svec{\nabla}^{2}\left(f_{0}^{\prime}(c)-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\svec{\nabla}^{2}c\right),\\ &\sqrt{\rho}\left(\sqrt{\rho}\svec{u}\right)_{t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho\svec{u}\svec{u}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\rho\svec{u}\cdot\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}+c\svec{\nabla}\mu=-\svec{\nabla}p+2\eta\mathsf{S}+\rho\svec{g},\\ &p_{t}+\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}\svec{\nabla}\cdot\svec{u}=0,\end{split} (115)

to describe the approximation in time.

The IMEX version of the BDF integrator for a time derivative d​y/d​tdy/dt is

γ0={1ifJ=132ifJ=2,y^={ynifJ=12​yn−12​yn−1ifJ=2,yn+1,e={ynifJ=12​yn−yn−1ifJ=2,\gamma_{0}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&\text{if}&J=1\\ \frac{3}{2}&\text{if}&J=2\end{array}\right.,~~\hat{y}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}y^{n}&\text{if}&J=1\\ 2y^{n}-\frac{1}{2}y^{n-1}&\text{if}&J=2\end{array}\right.,~~y^{n+1,e}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}y^{n}&\text{if}&J=1\\ 2y^{n}-y^{n-1}&\text{if}&J=2\end{array}\right., (116)

where yn=y⁡(tn)y^{n}=y(t_{n}), γ0\gamma_{0} and y^\hat{y} yield a JJ–th order approximation of the time derivative,

ytn+1≈γ0​yn+1−y^Δ​t,y_{t}^{n+1}\approx\frac{\gamma_{0}y^{n+1}-\hat{y}}{\Delta t}, (117)

and yn+1,ey^{n+1,e} is a JJ–th order explicit approximation of yn+1y^{n+1}. The IMEX scheme used in [24] was constructed to solve the fourth order derivative implicitly, and the remaining terms explicitly,

γ0​cn+1−c^Δ​t+∇→⋅(c​u→)n+1,e=M0​∇→2​(f0′​(cn+1,e)−32​σ​ε​∇→2​cn+1),ρn+1,e​γ0​ρ​u→n+1− ρ​u→      ^       Δ​t+(∇→⋅(12​ρ​u→​u→)+12​ρ​u→⋅∇→​u→+c​∇→​μ)n+1,e=(−∇→​p+2​η​𝖲+ρ​g→)n+1,e,γ0​pn+1−p^Δ​t+ρ0​c02​∇→⋅u→n+1,e=0.\begin{split}\frac{\gamma_{0}c^{n+1}-\hat{c}}{\Delta t}+\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(c\svec{u}\right)^{n+1,e}&=M_{0}\svec{\nabla}^{2}\left(f_{0}^{\prime}(c^{n+1,e})-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\svec{\nabla}^{2}c^{n+1}\right),\\ \sqrt{\rho^{n+1,e}}\frac{\gamma_{0}\sqrt{\rho}\svec{u}^{n+1}-\hbox{\hskip 5.85417pt\hskip-5.85417pt\hbox{$\sqrt{\rho}\svec{u}$}\hskip-5.85417pt\hskip 0.0pt\raisebox{0.24445pt}{\hbox{$\hbox{\lx@scalerel@obj{\lx@scalerel@obj{\lx@scalerel@obj{\kern 0.1pt\mathchar 866\kern 0.1pt}}}}$}}\hskip 0.0pt\hskip 5.85417pt}}{\Delta t}+&\left(\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho\svec{u}\svec{u}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\rho\svec{u}\cdot\svec{\nabla}\svec{u}+c\svec{\nabla}\mu\right)^{n+1,e}\\ &=\left(-\svec{\nabla}p+2\eta\mathsf{S}+\rho\svec{g}\right)^{n+1,e},\\ \frac{\gamma_{0}p^{n+1}-\hat{p}}{\Delta t}+\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}\svec{\nabla}\cdot\svec{u}^{n+1,e}&=0.\end{split} (118)

As in the vast majority of BDF implementations, the first step is first order (J=1J=1), and the following steps can be maintained first or use second order (J=2J=2). Note that the Jacobian matrix associated with the fourth order derivative is constant in time. Hence, only one computation of its solution is required. In this work, we perform a single LU decomposition, and afterwards use Gauss substitution to solve the linear system at each time step, but other direct or iterative solvers could be used.

One can use a fully explicit time integrator if the time step restriction allows it (e.g. when the chemical characteristic time is large enough). We have also implemented a low–storage third–order Runge–Kutta method to explicitly solve the system [41].

4 Semi–discrete stability analysis

We prove the stability of the spatial discretization (93), by showing that it mimics a discrete version of the entropy conservation law (55). As in the continuous analysis, we do not study the effect of lower order source terms (𝐒=0\mathbf{S}=0). The entropy analysis reproduces the continuous analysis steps discretely. Therefore, we use proper choices for the test functions, which contract the system of equations into a single equation, to be shaped into an entropy equation. The latter is produced in four steps, as we study the time derivative terms, inviscid terms, viscous terms, and finally interior and physical boundary terms.

First, we follow [8] and take the time derivative of (93d),
