=\displaystyle= ∫∂e,N(𝐖T𝐅↔v⋆+𝐖⋆,T𝐅↔v−𝐖T𝐅↔v)⋅n→dS−⟨𝒥𝐆↔,𝐅↔v⟩E,N,\displaystyle\int_{\partial e,N}\left(\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}^{\star}+\mathbf{W}^{\star,T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}-\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S-\left\langle\mathcal{J}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{G}},\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right\rangle_{E,N}, (121a)
⟨𝒥​μ,Ct⟩E,N=\displaystyle\left\langle\mathcal{J}\mu,C_{t}\right\rangle_{E,N}= ⟨𝒥​F0′,Ct⟩E,N+32​σ​ε​⟨𝒥​G→c,t,G→c⟩E,N\displaystyle\left\langle\mathcal{J}F_{0}^{\prime},C_{t}\right\rangle_{E,N}+\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\left\langle\mathcal{J}\svec{G}_{c,t},\svec{G}_{c}\right\rangle_{E,N}
−∫∂e,N32σε(CtG→c⋆+Ct⋆G→c−CtG→c)⋅n→dS,\displaystyle-\int_{\partial e,N}\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\left(C_{t}\svec{{G}}_{c}^{\star}+C_{t}^{\star}\svec{G}_{c}-C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S, (121b)

to combine four equations into two. Under the assumption of exactness in time, we can use the chain rule on (121b),

⟨𝒥​F0′,Ct⟩E,N+32​σ​ε​⟨𝒥​G→c,t,G→c⟩E,N=⟨𝒥​(F0+34​σ​ε​|G→c|2)t,1⟩E,N=⟨𝒥​ℱt,1⟩E,N,\begin{split}\left\langle\mathcal{J}F_{0}^{\prime},C_{t}\right\rangle_{E,N}+\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\left\langle\mathcal{J}\svec{G}_{c,t},\svec{G}_{c}\right\rangle_{E,N}=&\left\langle\mathcal{J}\left(F_{0}+\frac{3}{4}\sigma\varepsilon|\svec{G}_{c}|^{2}\right)_{t},1\right\rangle_{E,N}\\ =&\left\langle\mathcal{J}\mathcal{F}_{t},1\right\rangle_{E,N},\end{split} (122)

to obtain the time derivative of the discrete approximation of the free–energy (7).

We complete the analysis by examining each term in (121) separately to get the semi–discrete entropy law. The rest of the section computes the terms as follows: the time derivative coefficients in Sec. 4.1, inviscid volume integrals in Sec. 4.2, viscous volume integrals in Sec. 4.3, and lastly boundary integrals in Sec. 4.4. The discrete entropy law is completed in Sec. 4.5.

4.1 Time derivative coefficients

We first study the discrete inner product containing time derivatives found in (121a). We expand the inner product,

⟨𝒥​𝐌¯​𝐐t,𝐖⟩E,N=⟨𝒥​Ct,μ⟩E,N+⟨𝒥​(ρ​U→)t,ρ​U→⟩E,N+1ρ0​c02​⟨𝒥​Pt,P⟩E,N,\left\langle\mathcal{J}\underline{\mathbf{M}}\mathbf{Q}_{t},\mathbf{W}\right\rangle_{E,N}=\left\langle\mathcal{J}C_{t},\mu\right\rangle_{E,N}+\left\langle\mathcal{J}\left(\sqrt{\rho}\svec{U}\right)_{t},\sqrt{\rho}\svec{U}\right\rangle_{E,N}+\frac{1}{\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}}\left\langle\mathcal{J}P_{t},P\right\rangle_{E,N}, (123)

into which we insert the discrete approximation of ⟨𝒥​Ct,μ⟩E,N\left\langle\mathcal{J}C_{t},\mu\right\rangle_{E,N} found in (121b), and apply the chain rule in time for the kinetic and artificial compressibility terms,

⟨𝒥​𝐌¯​𝐐t,𝐖⟩E,N=⟨𝒥ℱt,1⟩E,N−∫∂e,N32σε(CtG→c⋆+Ct⋆G→c−CtG→c)⋅n→dS+⟨𝒥​(12​ρ​Vt​o​t2)t,1⟩E,N+⟨𝒥​(P22​ρ0​c02)t,1⟩E,N=⟨𝒥​(ℱ+𝒦+ℰAC)t,1⟩E,N−∫∂e,N32σε(CtG→c⋆+Ct⋆G→c−CtG→c)⋅n→dS=⟨𝒥ℰt,1⟩E,N−∫∂e,N32σε(CtG→c⋆+Ct⋆G→c−CtG→c)⋅n→dS.\begin{split}\left\langle\mathcal{J}\underline{\mathbf{M}}\mathbf{Q}_{t},\mathbf{W}\right\rangle_{E,N}=&\left\langle\mathcal{J}\mathcal{F}_{t},1\right\rangle_{E,N}-\int_{\partial e,N}\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\left(C_{t}\svec{{G}}_{c}^{\star}+C_{t}^{\star}\svec{G}_{c}-C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\\ &+\left\langle\mathcal{J}\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho V_{tot}^{2}\right)_{t},1\right\rangle_{E,N}+\left\langle\mathcal{J}\left(\frac{P^{2}}{2\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}}\right)_{t},1\right\rangle_{E,N}\\ =&\left\langle\mathcal{J}\left(\mathcal{F}+\mathcal{K}+\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{AC}}\right)_{t},1\right\rangle_{E,N}\\ &-\int_{\partial e,N}\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\left(C_{t}\svec{{G}}_{c}^{\star}+C_{t}^{\star}\svec{G}_{c}-C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\\ =&\left\langle\mathcal{J}\mathcal{E}_{t},1\right\rangle_{E,N}-\int_{\partial e,N}\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\left(C_{t}\svec{{G}}_{c}^{\star}+C_{t}^{\star}\svec{G}_{c}-C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S.\end{split} (124)

Eq. (124) is the discrete version of (39). As a result, we get the discrete version of (39) for the entropy,

ℰ=ℱ+𝒦+ℰA​C=F0+34​σ​ε​|G→c|2+12​ρ​Vt​o​t2+P22​ρ0​c02,\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{F}+\mathcal{K}+\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{A}C}=F_{0}+\frac{3}{4}\sigma\varepsilon|\svec{G}_{c}|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\rho V_{tot}^{2}+\frac{P^{2}}{2\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}}, (125)

and for the time entropy flux F→tℰ\svec{F}^{\mathcal{E}}_{t}, which appears as the argument of the surface integral in (124).

4.2 Inviscid volume terms

We now show that the contraction of the inviscid volume terms into a boundary entropy flux holds discretely as in the continuous analysis (47), i.e.,

⟨𝐖,∇→ξ⋅𝐅~↔e⟩E,N+∑m=15⟨𝐖,𝚽~↔m⋅∇→ξWm⟩E,N=∫∂e,NF→ℰ⋅n→dS.\left\langle\mathbf{W},\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\mathbf{F}}}_{e}\right\rangle_{E,N}+\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left\langle\mathbf{W},\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}}_{m}\cdot\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}W_{m}\right\rangle_{E,N}=\int_{\partial e,N}\svec{F}^{\mathcal{E}}\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S. (126)

Two properties were used in the continuous analysis: the integration by parts (which holds discretely by the discrete Gauss law (88)), and the relationship between inviscid fluxes and non–conservative terms (44), which also holds for contravariant components,

𝐞mT​𝐅~↔e=𝐞mT​(ℳT​𝐅↔e)=𝖬T​(𝐞mT​𝐅↔e)=𝖬T​(𝐖T​𝚽↔m)=𝐖T​(ℳT​𝚽↔m)=𝐖T​𝚽~↔m.\mathbf{e}_{m}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\mathbf{F}}}_{e}=\mathbf{e}_{m}^{T}\left(\mathcal{M}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}\right)=\mathsf{M}^{T}\left(\mathbf{e}_{m}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}\right)=\mathsf{M}^{T}\left(\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}_{m}\right)=\mathbf{W}^{T}\left(\mathcal{M}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}_{m}\right)=\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}}_{m}. (127)

In (127), space and state multiplications commute since the matrix (67) is built from identity matrices state–wise.

Eq. (127) together with the discrete Gauss law (88) is sufficient to prove (126). We use the discrete Gauss law for the first term in (126), and explicitly write the scalar product of the resulting integral approximation as the sum of the components,

⟨𝐖,∇→ξ⋅𝐅~↔e⟩E,N=∫∂e,N𝐖T𝐅↔e⋅n→dS−⟨𝐅~↔e,∇→ξ𝐖⟩E,N=∫∂e,N𝐖T𝐅↔e⋅n→dS−∑m=15⟨𝐞mT𝐅~↔e,∇→ξWm⟩E,N=∫∂e,NF→ℰ⋅n→dS−∑m=15⟨𝐖T𝚽~↔m,∇→ξWm⟩E,N.\begin{split}\left\langle\mathbf{W},\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\mathbf{F}}}_{e}\right\rangle_{E,N}=&\int_{\partial e,N}\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S-\left\langle\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\mathbf{F}}}_{e},\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}\mathbf{W}\right\rangle_{E,N}\\ =&\int_{\partial e,N}\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S-\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left\langle\mathbf{e}_{m}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\mathbf{F}}}_{e},\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}W_{m}\right\rangle_{E,N}\\ =&\int_{\partial e,N}\svec{F}^{\mathcal{E}}\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S-\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left\langle\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\tilde{\mathbf{\Phi}}}_{m},\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}W_{m}\right\rangle_{E,N}.\end{split} (128)

In the last identity, we used (45) and (127). Thus, when we move the non–conservative terms to the left hand side of (128), we prove (126).

4.3 Viscous volume terms

Analogously to (51), viscous volume terms are dissipative if

⟨𝒥​𝐆↔,𝐅↔v​(𝐆↔)⟩E,N⩾0.\left\langle\mathcal{J}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{G}},\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{G}}\right)\right\rangle_{E,N}\geqslant 0. (129)

Thus, we closely follow the continuous steps,

⟨𝒥​𝐆↔,𝐅↔v⟩E,N=M0​⟨𝒥​G→μ,G→μ⟩E,N+⟨𝒥​G→u→,2​η​𝒮⟩E,N=M0​⟨𝒥​G→μ,G→μ⟩E,N+⟨𝒥⁡(G→u→+G→u→T2),2​η​𝒮⟩E,N=⟨𝒥⁡(M0​|G→μ|2+2​η​𝒮:𝒮),1⟩E,N⩾0,\begin{split}\left\langle\mathcal{J}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{G}},\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right\rangle_{E,N}&=M_{0}\left\langle\mathcal{J}\svec{G}_{\mu},\svec{G}_{\mu}\right\rangle_{E,N}+\left\langle\mathcal{J}\svec{G}_{\svec{u}},2\eta\mathcal{S}\right\rangle_{E,N}\\ &=M_{0}\left\langle\mathcal{J}\svec{G}_{\mu},\svec{G}_{\mu}\right\rangle_{E,N}+\left\langle\mathcal{J}\left(\frac{\svec{G}_{\svec{u}}+\svec{G}_{\svec{u}}^{T}}{2}\right),2\eta\mathcal{S}\right\rangle_{E,N}\\ &=\left\langle\mathcal{J}\left(M_{0}|\svec{G}_{\mu}|^{2}+2\eta\mathcal{S}:\mathcal{S}\right),1\right\rangle_{E,N}\geqslant 0,\end{split} (130)

where 𝒮=𝖲⁡(G→u→)\mathcal{S}=\mathsf{S}\left(\svec{G}_{\svec{u}}\right) is the strain tensor (21) evaluated with the discrete gradients G→u→\svec{G}_{\svec{u}}. As a result, we find that discrete viscous volume terms are dissipative.

4.4 Boundary terms

Boundary term stability only makes sense when considering all elements in the domain. Thus, we update (121) with (124), (126), and (130), and sum over all elements, creating

⁡d​ℰ¯⁡d​t+IBT+PBT=−∑e⟨𝒥(M0|G→μ|2+2η𝒮:𝒮),1⟩E,N,\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathcal{E}}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t}+\mathrm{IBT}+\mathrm{PBT}=-\sum_{e}\left\langle\mathcal{J}\left(M_{0}|\svec{G}_{\mu}|^{2}+2\eta\mathcal{S}:\mathcal{S}\right),1\right\rangle_{E,N}, (131)

where ℰ¯\bar{\mathcal{E}} is the total entropy,

ℰ¯=∑e⟨𝒥​ℰ,1⟩E,N,\bar{\mathcal{E}}=\sum_{e}\left\langle\mathcal{J}\mathcal{E},1\right\rangle_{E,N}, (132)

IBT is the contribution from interior faces,

IBT=IBTe+IBTv+IBTc​h=−∑interiorfaces∫f,N(⟦𝐖T⟧𝐅↔e⋆+∑m=15⟦𝐖T(𝚽↔mWm)♢⟧−⟦𝐖T𝚽↔mWm⟧)⋅n→LdS+∑interiorfaces∫f,N(⟦𝐖T⟧𝐅↔v⋆+⟦𝐖T𝐅↔v⟧−𝐖⋆,T⟦F→v⟧)⋅n→LdS+32σε∑interiorfaces∫f,N(⟦Ct⟧G→c⋆+⟦G→c⟧Ct⋆−⟦CtG→c⟧)⋅n→LdS,\begin{split}\mathrm{IBT}=&\mathrm{IBT}_{e}+\mathrm{IBT}_{v}+\mathrm{IBT}_{ch}\\ =&-\sum_{{\mathrm{interior}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\right\rrbracket\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}^{\star}+\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right)^{\diamondsuit}\right\rrbracket-\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right\rrbracket\right)\cdot\svec{n}_{L}\mathrm{d}S\\ &+\sum_{{\mathrm{interior}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\right\rrbracket\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}^{\star}+\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right\rrbracket-\mathbf{W}^{\star,T}\left\llbracket\svec{F}_{v}\right\rrbracket\right)\cdot\svec{n}_{L}\mathrm{d}S\\ &+\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\sum_{{\mathrm{interior}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\left\llbracket C_{t}\right\rrbracket\svec{G}_{c}^{\star}+\left\llbracket\svec{G}_{c}\right\rrbracket C_{t}^{\star}-\left\llbracket C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}\right\rrbracket\right)\cdot\svec{n}_{L}\mathrm{d}S,\\ \end{split} (133)

and PBT is the contribution from physical boundary faces,

PBT=PBTe+PBTv+PBTc​h=∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(𝐖T​𝐅↔e⋆+∑m=15𝐖T​((𝚽↔m​Wm)♢−𝚽↔m​Wm))⋅n→​𝑑S−∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(𝐖T(𝐅↔v⋆−𝐅↔v)+𝐖⋆,T𝐅↔v)⋅n→dS−32σε∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(CtG→c⋆+C⋆tG→c−CtG→c)⋅n→dS.\begin{split}\mathrm{PBT}=&\mathrm{PBT}_{e}+\mathrm{PBT}_{v}+\mathrm{PBT}_{ch}\\ =&\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}^{\star}+\sum_{m=1}^{5}\mathbf{W}^{T}\left(\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right)^{\diamondsuit}-\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right)\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathrm{d}S\\ &-\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\mathbf{W}^{T}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}^{\star}-\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right)+\mathbf{W}^{\star,T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathrm{d}S\\ &-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}^{\star}+C^{\star}_{t}\svec{G}_{c}-C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S.\end{split} (134)

In the inviscid fluxes, the entropy flux definition F→ℰ=𝐖T​𝐅↔e\svec{F}^{\mathcal{E}}=\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e} was taken into account to reduce the number of terms. Moreover, in the interior boundary terms, we used the left element as the reference (hence the n→L\svec{n}_{L} vector).

We now analyze the contributions of the interior and boundary terms in (131) separately.

4.4.1 Inviscid interior boundary terms: entropy conserving scheme with central fluxes

We address the stability of the inviscid interior boundary terms when using the central fluxes for the conservative numerical (100) and non–conservative diamond fluxes (101). Inserting the central fluxes into the inviscid IBTe\mathrm{IBT}_{e} (133) terms,

IBTe=−∑interiorfaces∫f,N(⟦𝐖T⟧𝐅↔e⋆+∑m=15⟦𝐖T(𝚽↔mWm)♢⟧−⟦𝐖T𝚽↔mWm⟧)⋅n→LdS=−∑interiorfaces∫f,N(⟦𝐖T⟧{{𝐅↔e}}+∑m=15⟦𝐖T𝚽↔m⟧{{Wm}}−⟦𝐖T𝚽↔mWm⟧)⋅n→LdS=−∑interiorfaces∫f,N∑m=15(⟦Wm⟧{{𝐞Tm𝐅↔e}}−⟦Wm⟧{{𝐖T𝚽↔m}})⋅n→LdS=0.\begin{split}\mathrm{IBT}_{e}=&-\sum_{{\mathrm{interior}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\right\rrbracket\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}^{\star}+\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right)^{\diamondsuit}\right\rrbracket-\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right\rrbracket\right)\cdot\svec{n}_{L}\mathrm{d}S\\ =&-\sum_{{\mathrm{interior}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\right\rrbracket\{\!\{\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}\}\!\}+\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}\right\rrbracket\{\!\{W_{m}\}\!\}-\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right\rrbracket\right)\cdot\svec{n}_{L}\mathrm{d}S\\ =&-\sum_{{\mathrm{interior}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left(\left\llbracket{W}_{m}\right\rrbracket\{\!\{\mathbf{e}^{T}_{m}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}\}\!\}-\left\llbracket W_{m}\right\rrbracket\{\!\{\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}\}\!\}\right)\cdot\svec{n}_{L}\mathrm{d}S=0.\\ \end{split} (135)

Thus we find that inviscid interior boundaries exactly satisfy IBTe=0\mathrm{IBT}_{e}=0. In the second equality, we explicitly wrote the first product as the sum of the product of its components, and in the last equality, we used the algebraic relationship satisfied by jump and average operators,

⟦u​v⟧={{u}}​⟦v⟧+⟦u⟧​{{v}}\left\llbracket uv\right\rrbracket=\{\!\{u\}\!\}\left\llbracket v\right\rrbracket+\left\llbracket u\right\rrbracket\{\!\{v\}\!\} (136)

for the second and third products. Additionally, both terms in the last sum of (135) are identical because of the condition (44). We conclude that inviscid interior boundary contribution to the entropy equation is identically zero, i.e. the interface approximation is entropy conserving.

4.4.2 Inviscid interior boundary terms: entropy stable scheme with the exact Riemann solver

The exact Riemann solver was proven to be stable in [9] for the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations. Now we extend the proof to the iNS/CH system, which is done by a consistent choice of the diamond fluxes. The proof rests on the exact Riemann solver star solution satisfying

ΔeERS=12​ρ⋆​⟦Vt​o​t2⟧​Un⋆−ρ⋆​Un⋆​(Un⋆​⟦Un⟧+Vt​1⋆​⟦Vt​1⟧+Vt​2⋆​⟦Vt​2⟧)−P⋆​⟦Un⟧−⟦P⟧​Un⋆+⟦P​Un⟧⩾0.\begin{split}\Delta_{e}^{\mathrm{ERS}}=&\frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}\left\llbracket V_{tot}^{2}\right\rrbracket U_{n}^{\star}-\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}\left(U_{n}^{\star}\left\llbracket U_{n}\right\rrbracket+V_{t1}^{\star}\left\llbracket V_{t1}\right\rrbracket+V_{t2}^{\star}\left\llbracket V_{t2}\right\rrbracket\right)\\ &-P^{\star}\left\llbracket U_{n}\right\rrbracket-\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket U_{n}^{\star}+\left\llbracket PU_{n}\right\rrbracket\geqslant 0.\end{split} (137)

Eq. (137) implies that the ERS is dissipative for the incompressible NSE. We use the same star region solution for the inviscid numerical fluxes (105) and the choice for the diamond fluxes given in (106). The result is that the argument of the inviscid interior boundary terms is

ΔeIBT=(−⟦𝐖T⟧​𝐅↔e⋆−∑m=15⟦𝐖T​(𝚽↔m​Wm)♢⟧+⟦𝐖T​𝚽↔m​Wm⟧)⋅n→L=−⟦𝐖T⟧​𝐓¯T​𝐅e⋆−⟦𝐖T​𝐓¯T​𝐅Φ​WERS⟧+⟦𝐖T​𝐓¯T​𝐅Φ​W⟧=−⟦𝐖nT⟧​𝐅e⋆−⟦𝐖nT​(𝐅Φ​WERS−𝐅Φ​W)⟧.\begin{split}\Delta_{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathrm{IBT}}=&\left(-\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\right\rrbracket\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}^{\star}-\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right)^{\diamondsuit}\right\rrbracket+\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right\rrbracket\right)\cdot\svec{n}_{L}\\ =&-\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\right\rrbracket\underline{\mathbf{T}}^{T}\mathbf{F}_{e}^{\star}-\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\underline{\mathbf{T}}^{T}\mathbf{F}_{\Phi W}^{\mathrm{ERS}}\right\rrbracket+\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\underline{\mathbf{T}}^{T}\mathbf{F}_{\Phi W}\right\rrbracket\\ =&-\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}_{n}^{T}\right\rrbracket\mathbf{F}_{e}^{\star}-\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}_{n}^{T}\left(\mathbf{F}_{\Phi W}^{\mathrm{ERS}}-\mathbf{F}_{\Phi W}\right)\right\rrbracket.\end{split} (138)

We write the first term in the last line of (138) as

−⟦𝐖nT⟧​𝐅e⋆=−⟦μ⟧​{{C​Un}}−12​ρ⋆​Un⋆​(Un⋆​⟦Un⟧+Vt​1⋆​⟦Vt​1⟧+Vt​2⋆​⟦Vt​2⟧)−P⋆​⟦Un⟧,-\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}_{n}^{T}\right\rrbracket\mathbf{F}_{e}^{\star}=-\left\llbracket\mu\right\rrbracket\{\!\{CU_{n}\}\!\}-\frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}\left(U_{n}^{\star}\left\llbracket U_{n}\right\rrbracket+V_{t1}^{\star}\left\llbracket V_{t1}\right\rrbracket+V_{t2}^{\star}\left\llbracket V_{t2}\right\rrbracket\right)-P^{\star}\left\llbracket U_{n}\right\rrbracket, (139)

and the second term as

−⟦𝐖nT​(𝐅Φ​WERS−𝐅Φ​W)⟧=−12​ρ⋆​Un⋆,2​⟦Un⟧+12​ρ⋆​Un⋆​⟦Un2⟧−{{μ}}​⟦C​Un⟧+⟦C​Un​μ⟧−12​ρ⋆​Un⋆​Vt​1⋆​⟦Vt​1⟧+12​ρ⋆​Un⋆​⟦Vt​12⟧−12​ρ⋆​Un⋆​Vt​2⋆​⟦Vt​2⟧+12​ρ⋆​Un⋆​⟦Vt​22⟧−Un⋆​⟦P⟧+⟦P​Un⟧=12​ρ⋆​Un⋆​⟦Vt​o​t2⟧+⟦μ⟧​{{C​Un}}−12​ρ⋆​Un⋆​(Un⋆​⟦Un⟧+Vt​1⋆​⟦Vt​1⟧+Vt​2⋆​⟦Vt​2⟧)−Un⋆​⟦P⟧+⟦P​Un⟧,\begin{split}-\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}_{n}^{T}\left(\mathbf{F}_{\Phi W}^{\mathrm{ERS}}-\mathbf{F}_{\Phi W}\right)\right\rrbracket=&-\frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star,2}\left\llbracket U_{n}\right\rrbracket+\frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}\left\llbracket U_{n}^{2}\right\rrbracket-\{\!\{\mu\}\!\}\left\llbracket CU_{n}\right\rrbracket+\left\llbracket CU_{n}\mu\right\rrbracket\\ &-\frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}V_{t1}^{\star}\left\llbracket V_{t1}\right\rrbracket+\frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}\left\llbracket V_{t1}^{2}\right\rrbracket\\ &-\frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}V_{t2}^{\star}\left\llbracket V_{t2}\right\rrbracket+\frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}\left\llbracket V_{t2}^{2}\right\rrbracket\\ &-U_{n}^{\star}\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket+\left\llbracket PU_{n}\right\rrbracket\\ =&\frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}\left\llbracket V_{tot}^{2}\right\rrbracket+\left\llbracket\mu\right\rrbracket\{\!\{CU_{n}\}\!\}\\ &-\frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}\left(U_{n}^{\star}\left\llbracket U_{n}\right\rrbracket+V_{t1}^{\star}\left\llbracket V_{t1}\right\rrbracket+V_{t2}^{\star}\left\llbracket V_{t2}\right\rrbracket\right)\\ &-U_{n}^{\star}\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket+\left\llbracket PU_{n}\right\rrbracket,\end{split} (140)

which when inserted into (138) yields,

ΔeIBT=12​ρ⋆​Un⋆​⟦Vt​o​t⟧2−ρ⋆​Un⋆​(Un⋆​⟦Un⟧+Vt​1⋆​⟦Vt​1⟧+Vt​2⋆​⟦Vt​2⟧)−P⋆​⟦Un⟧−Un⋆​⟦P⟧+⟦P​Un⟧=ΔeERS⩾0.\begin{split}\Delta_{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathrm{IBT}}=&\frac{1}{2}\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}\left\llbracket V_{tot}\right\rrbracket^{2}-\rho^{\star}U_{n}^{\star}\left(U_{n}^{\star}\left\llbracket U_{n}\right\rrbracket+V_{t1}^{\star}\left\llbracket V_{t1}\right\rrbracket+V_{t2}^{\star}\left\llbracket V_{t2}\right\rrbracket\right)\\ &-P^{\star}\left\llbracket U_{n}\right\rrbracket-U_{n}^{\star}\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket+\left\llbracket PU_{n}\right\rrbracket=\Delta_{e}^{\mathrm{ERS}}\geqslant 0.\end{split} (141)

The non–negativity of ΔeIBT\Delta_{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathrm{IBT}} confirms that the incompressible NSE exact Riemann solver (105), with the associated diamond flux choice (106) introduced in this work produces an entropy stable interface approximation for the iNS/CH system.

4.4.3 Viscous and Cahn–Hilliard interior terms: Bassi–Rebay 1 method

The use of the standard BR1 method identically cancels the boundary integrals (see [16] for the compressible NSE, [9] for the incompressible NSE, [37] for the MHD equations, and [8] for the Cahn–Hilliard equation). Then, we prove that the extra interface stabilization terms are dissipative. In this work, we obtain the same integral approximation as in [9] for the incompressible NSE, and as in [8] for the Cahn–Hilliard part,

IBTv=∑interiorfaces∫f,N(⟦𝐖T⟧​𝐅↔v⋆−⟦𝐖T​𝐅↔v⟧+𝐖⋆,T​⟦𝐅↔v⟧)⋅n→L​𝑑S=∑interiorfaces∫f,N(⟦𝐖T⟧​{{𝐅↔v}}+β​⟦μ⟧2​n→L−⟦𝐖T​𝐅↔v⟧+{{𝐖}}T​⟦𝐅↔v⟧)⋅n→L​𝑑S=∑interiorfaces∫f,Nβ​⟦μ⟧2​dS⩾0,\begin{split}\mathrm{IBT}_{v}=&\sum_{{\mathrm{interior}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\right\rrbracket\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}^{\star}-\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right\rrbracket+\mathbf{W}^{\star,T}\left\llbracket\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right\rrbracket\right)\cdot\svec{n}_{L}\mathrm{d}S\\ =&\sum_{{\mathrm{interior}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\right\rrbracket\{\!\{\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\}\!\}+\beta\left\llbracket\mu\right\rrbracket^{2}\svec{n}_{L}-\left\llbracket\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right\rrbracket+\{\!\{\mathbf{W}\}\!\}^{T}\left\llbracket\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right\rrbracket\right)\cdot\svec{n}_{L}\mathrm{d}S\\ =&\sum_{{\mathrm{interior}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\beta\left\llbracket\mu\right\rrbracket^{2}\mathrm{d}S\geqslant 0,\end{split} (142)

whereas for the Cahn–Hilliard terms,

IBTc​h=32​σ​ε​∑interiorfaces∫f,N(⟦Ct⟧​G→c⋆+⟦G→c⟧​Ct⋆−⟦Ct​G→c⟧)⋅n→L​𝑑S=32​σ​ε​∑interiorfaces∫f,N(⟦Ct⟧​{{G→c}}+⟦G→c⟧​{{Ct}}+β⁡⟦C⟧​⟦Ct⟧​n→L−⟦Ct​G→c⟧)⋅n→L​𝑑S=34​σ​ε​⁡d⁡d​t​∑interiorfaces∫f,Nβ​⟦C⟧2​dS,\begin{split}\mathrm{IBT}_{ch}=&\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\sum_{{\mathrm{interior}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\left\llbracket C_{t}\right\rrbracket\svec{G}_{c}^{\star}+\left\llbracket\svec{G}_{c}\right\rrbracket C_{t}^{\star}-\left\llbracket C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}\right\rrbracket\right)\cdot\svec{n}_{L}\mathrm{d}S\\ =&\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\sum_{{\mathrm{interior}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\left\llbracket C_{t}\right\rrbracket\{\!\{\svec{G}_{c}\}\!\}+\left\llbracket\svec{G}_{c}\right\rrbracket\{\!\{C_{t}\}\!\}+\beta\left\llbracket C\right\rrbracket\left\llbracket C_{t}\right\rrbracket\svec{n}_{L}-\left\llbracket C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}\right\rrbracket\right)\cdot\svec{n}_{L}\mathrm{d}S\\ =&\frac{3}{4}\sigma\varepsilon\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t}\sum_{{\mathrm{interior}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\beta\left\llbracket C\right\rrbracket^{2}\mathrm{d}S,\\ \end{split} (143)

which says that viscous and Cahn–Hilliard interior boundary contributions do not contribute to the entropy balance if β=0\beta=0, since the integrals are identically zero. This means that interface stabilization is not a requirement for stability. When β>0\beta>0, the integrals in IBTv\mathrm{IBT}_{v} are positive (i.e. dissipative), and the integral in IBTc​h\mathrm{IBT}_{ch}, which is not positive per se because of the time derivative, will be added to the entropy, since the integral argument is positive.

4.4.4 Interior boundary terms: Summary

The contribution to the interior boundary terms from viscous and Cahn–Hilliard terms are identically zero when using the BR1 method without interface stabilization (β=0\beta=0), and dissipative otherwise (β>0\beta>0). As for the inviscid terms, interior boundary terms are conservative with central fluxes (IBTe=0\mathrm{IBT}_{e}=0), and dissipative with the exact Riemann solver (IBTe⩾0\mathrm{IBT}_{e}\geqslant 0).

4.4.5 Physical boundary terms: free– and no–slip walls

We now address the stability of physical wall boundary terms (134). For inviscid fluxes PBTe\mathrm{PBT}_{e}, we use the entropy conserving approach with central fluxes (110),

PBTe=∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(𝐖T​𝐅↔e⋆+∑m=15𝐖T​((𝚽↔m​Wm)♢−𝚽↔m​Wm))⋅n→​𝑑S=∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(Un​(12​ρ​Un2+P)+Un​(μ​C−12​ρ​Un−μ​C)−P​Un)​⁡dS=0,\begin{split}\mathrm{PBT}_{e}&=\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}^{\star}+\sum_{m=1}^{5}\mathbf{W}^{T}\left(\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right)^{\diamondsuit}-\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right)\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathrm{d}S\\ &=\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(U_{n}\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}^{2}+P\right)+U_{n}\left(\mu C-\frac{1}{2}\rho U_{n}-\mu C\right)-PU_{n}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S=0,\end{split} (144)

or the entropy stable counterpart with the exact Riemann solver (112),

PBTe=∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(𝐖T​𝐅↔e⋆+∑m=15𝐖T​((𝚽↔m​Wm)♢−𝚽↔m​Wm))⋅n→​𝑑S=∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(Un​(12​ρ​λ+​Un+P)−P​Un)​⁡dS=∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(12​ρ​λ+​Un2)​⁡dS⩾0.\begin{split}\mathrm{PBT}_{e}&=\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}^{\star}+\sum_{m=1}^{5}\mathbf{W}^{T}\left(\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right)^{\diamondsuit}-\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right)\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathrm{d}S\\ &=\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(U_{n}\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho\lambda^{+}U_{n}+P\right)-PU_{n}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S=\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho\lambda^{+}U_{n}^{2}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\geqslant 0.\end{split} (145)

Either way, the inviscid physical boundary contribution is stable. Furthermore, for the viscous terms, the free–slip wall boundary condition (113),

PBTv=−∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(𝐖T(𝐅↔v⋆−𝐅↔v)+𝐖⋆,T𝐅↔v)⋅n→dS−∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(𝐖T(0−𝐅↔v)+𝐖T𝐅↔v)⋅n→dS=0,\begin{split}\mathrm{PBT}_{v}=&-\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\mathbf{W}^{T}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}^{\star}-\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right)+\mathbf{W}^{\star,T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathrm{d}S\\ &-\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\mathbf{W}^{T}\left({0}-\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right)+\mathbf{W}^{T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathrm{d}S=0,\end{split} (146)

and for the no–slip wall boundary condition (114),

PBTv=−∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(𝐖T(𝐅↔v⋆−𝐅↔v)+𝐖⋆,T𝐅↔v)⋅n→dS−∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(−μG→μ+μG→μ+U→𝒮−U→𝒮)⋅n→dS=0,\begin{split}\mathrm{PBT}_{v}=&-\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\mathbf{W}^{T}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}^{\star}-\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right)+\mathbf{W}^{\star,T}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{v}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathrm{d}S\\ &-\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(-\mu\svec{G}_{\mu}+\mu\svec{G}_{\mu}+\svec{U}\mathcal{S}-\svec{U}\mathcal{S}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathrm{d}S=0,\end{split} (147)

are dissipative. Lastly, the Cahn–Hilliard physical boundary condition for both free– and no–slip walls (113)–(114) gives,

PBTc​h=−32σε∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(CtG→c⋆+C⋆tG→c−CtG→c)⋅n→dS=−∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(−Ctfw′(C)+32σε(CtG→c−CtG→c))⋅n→dS=⁡d⁡d​t​∑boundaryfaces∫f,Nfw​(C)​⁡dS,\begin{split}\mathrm{PBT}_{ch}=&-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}^{\star}+C^{\star}_{t}\svec{G}_{c}-C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\\ =&-\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(-C_{t}f_{w}^{\prime}(C)+\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\left(C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}-C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}\right)\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\\ =&\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t}\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}f_{w}(C)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S,\end{split} (148)

which represents the discrete version of the surface free–energy time derivative (60).

4.5 Semi–discrete stability: Summary

We constructed a DG approximation of the iNS/CH system (93) whose analysis mimics the continuous stability analysis of Sec. 2.1 semi–discretely. As a result, we have shown that the discrete entropy satisfies a balance law,

⁡d⁡d​t(ℰ¯β+∑boundaryfaces∫f,Nfw(C)dS)⩽−∑e⟨𝒥(M0|G→μ|2+2η𝒮:𝒮),1⟩E,N,\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t}\left(\bar{\mathcal{E}}^{\beta}+\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}f_{w}(C)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\right)\leqslant-\sum_{e}\left\langle\mathcal{J}\left(M_{0}|\svec{G}_{\mu}|^{2}+2\eta\mathcal{S}:\mathcal{S}\right),1\right\rangle_{E,N}, (149)

for both free– and no–slip wall boundary conditions. The entropy has been extended to consider the interface stabilization in the Cahn–Hilliard equation,

ℰ¯β=∑e⟨𝒥​ℰ,1⟩E,N+34​σ​ε​∑interiorfaces∫f,Nβ​⟦C⟧2​𝑑S⩾0.\bar{\mathcal{E}}^{\beta}=\sum_{e}\left\langle\mathcal{J}\mathcal{E},1\right\rangle_{E,N}+\frac{3}{4}\sigma\varepsilon\sum_{{\mathrm{interior}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\beta\left\llbracket C\right\rrbracket^{2}\mathrm{d}S\geqslant 0. (150)

Note that if β=0\beta=0 we recover ℰ¯β=0=ℰ¯=∑e⟨𝒥​ℰ,1⟩E,N\bar{\mathcal{E}}^{\beta=0}=\bar{\mathcal{E}}=\sum_{e}\left\langle\mathcal{J}\mathcal{E},1\right\rangle_{E,N}, and that a continuous solution (i.e. ⟦C⟧=0\left\llbracket C\right\rrbracket=0) also recovers the original entropy. Otherwise, the extended entropy ℰ¯β\bar{\mathcal{E}}^{\beta} is also always positive, such that its definition remains valid and the scheme is entropy–stable. The justification to include this term in the entropy, is that the free–energy measures the fluid interfaces using the solution gradients 34​σ​ε​|G→c|2\frac{3}{4}\sigma\varepsilon|\svec{G}_{c}|^{2}. However, if the discrete solution is allowed to be discontinuous at the inter–elements interface, it enables the creation of a fluid interface, which is not reflected in the original free–energy. The addition of this penalization, allows to account for inter–element discontinuities as part of the fluid interface, so that their associated energy is also weighted in the entropy. In practice, we have found that if the flow is under–resolved and β=0\beta=0, the solution minimizes the entropy allowing sharp discontinuities at the inter–elements interface. Since that effect has not been taken into account in the entropy with β=0\beta=0, the flow wrongly enables the discontinuity mechanism to minimize the entropy. This adverse effect (from the point of view of accuracy) is mitigated when β>0\beta>0 [18, 8]. Since now the inter–elements discontinuities belong to the entropy, their size can be kept bounded and controlled. In any case, the use of interface stabilization does not compromise the stability of the scheme.

Finally, the form of (149) depends on the choice of the inviscid numerical and diamond fluxes, and the Cahn–Hilliard interface stabilization: an equality for central fluxes and β=0\beta=0, and an inequality for the exact Riemann solver and β>0\beta>0. For either choice, the discrete entropy plus the surface free energy remains bounded by the initial condition.

5 Numerical experiments

We now explore the capabilities of the new DGSEM with numerical simulations. First, we validate the implementation with a convergence study on a manufactured solution. Second, we explore the robustness of the scheme by integrating in time from a random initial condition, where we compare an entropy–stable scheme with a Gauss point formulation that is not provably stable. Third, we solve a static bubble as a benchmark for steady–state accuracy, and a transient rising bubble. Finally, we present solutions for a three–dimensional pipe flow in the annular regime.

5.1 Convergence study

We first assess the spatial and temporal accuracy of the implementation of the approximation. We test with the same two–dimensional manufactured solution and configuration used in other Navier–Stokes/Cahn–Hilliard works, specifically [24],

cm​(x,y,t)=12​(1+cos⁡(π​x)​cos⁡(π​y)​sin⁡(t)),um​(x,y,t)=2​sin⁡(π​x)​cos⁡(π​z)​sin⁡(t),vm​(x,y,t)=−2​cos⁡(π​x)​sin⁡(π​y)​sin⁡(t),pm​(x,y,t)=2​sin⁡(π​x)​sin⁡(π​z)​cos⁡(t),\begin{split}c_{m}(x,y;t)&=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\cos\left(\pi x\right)\cos\left(\pi y\right)\sin\left(t\right)\right),\\ u_{m}(x,y;t)&=2\sin\left(\pi x\right)\cos\left(\pi z\right)\sin\left(t\right),\\ v_{m}(x,y;t)&=-2\cos\left(\pi x\right)\sin\left(\pi y\right)\sin\left(t\right),\\ p_{m}(x,y;t)&=2\sin\left(\pi x\right)\sin\left(\pi z\right)\cos\left(t\right),\end{split} (151)

on the domain (x,y)∈[−1,1]2(x,y)\in[-1,1]^{2}. The final time is tF=0.1t_{F}=0.1, and all physical parameters are presented in Table 1.

We measure L2 errors using the discrete inner product,

error=‖ϕ−ϕm‖𝒥,N=∑e⟨𝒥⁡(Φ−Φm),(Φ−Φm)⟩E,N.\mathrm{error}=\|\phi-\phi_{m}\|_{\mathcal{J},N}=\sqrt{\sum_{e}\left\langle\mathcal{J}\left(\Phi-\Phi_{m}\right),\left(\Phi-\Phi_{m}\right)\right\rangle_{E,N}}. (152)

Regarding the configuration of the scheme, we use the exact Riemann solver, and we vary the polynomial order NN, mesh size (we use an equally spaced Cartesian mesh M2M^{2}), and time–step size Δ​t\Delta t of the BDF2 scheme (J=2J=2) to evaluate the convergence rates as the resolution is increased either by increasing the polynomial order or decreasing the mesh size.

We first use a Cartesian 424^{2} element mesh and vary the polynomial order from N=3N=3 to 10. The L2 errors (152) are presented in Fig. 1, using Δ​t=10−4\Delta t=10^{-4} in Fig. 1(a) and Δ​t=10−5\Delta t=10^{-5} in Fig. 1(b).

Figs. 1(a) and 1(b) show typical and expected error behavior: an approximately linear semi-log convergence for lower polynomial orders implying exponential convergence of the error (i.e. under–resolved solution in space), and error stagnation for higher orders (under–resolved solution in time). The stagnation error threshold can be controlled with Δ​t\Delta t, as shown in Fig. 1(b).

For the next test configuration, we use polynomial orders N=2,3,4N=2,3,4 and 55, and meshes with 42,62,82,1224^{2},6^{2},8^{2},12^{2} and 16216^{2} elements for an h−h-type convergence study. The time–step is Δ​t=5⋅10−5\Delta t=5\cdot 10^{-5}. We solve the manufactured solution problem (151), and summarize the errors in Table 2. An estimate of the scheme’s order of convergence is provided there. We note that for the momentum components, the convergence orders are as expected, as they are close to N+1N+1. For the pressure, the order of convergence is somewhat smaller (closer to NN), which was also experienced in [25, 9]. The convergence is also not optimal for the concentration; for even polynomials, the convergence can surpass the theoretical N+1N+1 value, while for odd polynomials, the convergence rate is roughly NN in most of the cases. This effect was also noticed in [8], whose nature remains unclear.

5.2 Assessing robustness: random initial condition

We also assess the robustness of the scheme by introducing a random initial condition. Because the scheme developed here is entropy stable even for severely under–resolved solutions, the numerical implementation should not crash, as long as the time–step is small enough to stay within the time integrator stability region and the positivity condition is satisfied.

As a point of reference, and only in this section, we also consider the DG scheme using Gauss points. The standard DG method with Gauss points does not satisfy the SAT property [35] and the proofs developed for semi–discrete stability do not carry over. As a result, the standard scheme is not provably stable. To make the comparison even more stark, we compare robustness of the Gauss scheme with upwind flux dissipation to the new Gauss–Lobatto method with only central fluxes.

We solve the problem on the domain Ω=[0,1]3\Omega=[0,1]^{3}, and on a three–dimensional 434^{3} element Cartesian mesh. We initialize the solution using uniform random numbers in [0,1][0,1] for concentration, and in [−1,1][-1,1] for velocities and pressure. We use a high density ratio (ρ1/ρ2=1000\rho_{1}/\rho_{2}=1000), and Reynolds number R​e=106Re=10^{6} so that physical viscosity will have only a weak stabilizing effect. The rest of the parameters are given in Table 3.

With Gauss–Lobatto points, the discrete entropy balance (149) shows that the free–energy time derivative ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t} should be always negative as a result of viscous and chemical potential dissipation, for either central fluxes or the ERS. Moreover, the entropy remainder, defined as

ℛ⁡(ℰ)=⁡d⁡d​t​(∑e⟨𝒥​ℰ,1⟩E,N+∑boundaryfaces∫f,Nfw​(C)​⁡𝑑S)+⟨𝒥⁡(M0​|G→μ|2+2​η​𝒮:𝒮),1⟩E,N⩽0,\mathcal{R}\left(\mathcal{E}\right)=\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t}\left(\sum_{e}\left\langle\mathcal{J}\mathcal{E},1\right\rangle_{E,N}+\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}f_{w}(C)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\right)+\left\langle\mathcal{J}\left(M_{0}|\svec{G}_{\mu}|^{2}+2\eta\mathcal{S}:\mathcal{S}\right),1\right\rangle_{E,N}\leqslant 0, (153)

should be zero at each time step for central fluxes, and negative for the ERS. None of the statements regarding ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t} or ℛ⁡(ℰ)\mathcal{R}\left(\mathcal{E}\right) being negative are guaranteed to hold for Gauss points by theory.

The entropy time derivative evolution is presented in Fig. 2, and the entropy remainder (153) in Fig. 3.

Both are presented for three polynomial orders (N=2,3,4N=2,3,4), and for the three configurations described: Gauss–Lobatto points with ERS, Gauss–Lobatto points with central fluxes, and Gauss points with ERS. We find that the solutions follow the same pattern for the different polynomial orders. Gauss–Lobatto points are always stable, and the ERS enhances the stability (i.e. the entropy time derivative is always smaller or equal when compared to central fluxes). This is confirmed by looking at the entropy remainder in Fig. 3, which is machine precision for central fluxes, and negative for the ERS. Whereas for Gauss points, the solution is divergent (i.e. crashes) when t≥1.53t\geq 1.53. We see that for this case, Gauss points are more dissipative than Gauss–Lobatto points for the first steps, but then the opposite occurs when t>10−2t>10^{-2}.

With a random initial condition, the Gauss approximation is prone to diverge, but might not. We ran another 100100 random initial conditions with different seeds until a final time tF=10.0t_{F}=10.0, of which 30/100 crashed. For the 70 simulations that did not crash, most of them experienced growth of their entropy at some points in time. We represent in Fig. 4 the number of simulations that crashed before the physical time on the horizontal axis.

Most often crashes occur early, i.e. times t≈1.0t\approx 1.0, after which the simulation is less likely to crash. None of the simulations crashed if they stayed stable for more than 4.0 seconds. In other words, if it can be computed beyond the initial stages, it is more likely to continue.

We repeated the experiment for the entropy stable Gauss–Lobatto variant, to confirm that none of them crashed. There may be advantages to use Gauss points, because of higher accuracy per degree of freedom [42, 43], and indeed the scheme presented herein allows us to use Gauss points in practice. However, as it is not entropy stable, it might crash under certain conditions, perhaps severely under–resolved simulations like high Reynolds turbulent flows, etc.

5.3 Static bubble

In this test problem we solve a steady two–dimensional bubble and validate the pressure jump that results from surface tension. In the domain Ω=[0,1]×[0,1]\Omega=[0,1]\times[0,1], the initial condition for the concentration is

c⁡(x,y,0)=1−tanh⁡(−r−0.25ζ)2,r=(x−0.5)2+(y−0.5)2,ζ=2.5⋅10−3,c(x,y;0)=\frac{1-\tanh\left(-\frac{r-0.25}{\zeta}\right)}{2},~~r=\sqrt{(x-0.5)^{2}+(y-0.5)^{2}},~~\zeta=2.5\cdot 10^{-3}, (154)

which approximates a circle with radius R0=0.25R_{0}=0.25. Since we project the initial condition into our polynomial ansatz, the radius obtained, ReR_{e}, subtly differs to R0R_{0}. The analytical pressure jump between outside and inside of the bubble Δ​pa\Delta p_{a} is given by the Poisson law,

Δ​pa=pi−pe=p⁡(0.5,0.5)−p⁡(1.0,0.5)=σRe.\Delta p_{a}=p_{i}-p_{e}=p(0.5,0.5)-p(1.0,0.5)=\frac{\sigma}{R_{e}}. (155)

Note that we used the radius ReR_{e}, which is estimated from the final solution contour c⁡(x,y)=0.5c(x,y)=0.5, to compute the analytical solution. The rest of the parameters, including the surface tension σ=1\sigma=1 N/m, are given in Table 4.

We apply periodic boundary conditions at the four physical boundaries, and use the first order IMEX scheme (J=1J=1) until the residuals are kept lower than 10−710^{-7}.

The results are summarized in Table 5, which are computed with polynomial order N=2N=2 and three meshes 16216^{2}, 32232^{2}, and 64264^{2}. For all meshes, we compute the solution radius ReR_{e}, the analytical pressure jump Δ​pa\Delta p_{a}, which are compared to the numerical solution interior pressure, pip_{i}, exterior pressure pep_{e}, and pressure jump Δ​p\Delta p. Here we refer to the static pressure, and not the auxiliary pressure (16). The results show that the pressure jump converges to that given by the Poisson law (155) as we refine the grid.

In the last column of Table 5 we represent the norm of the velocity, which is of the size of the residuals. This implies that no parasitic currents are produced using this formulation, which are common in alternative Navier–Stokes/Cahn–Hilliard formulations [44]. Usually, the size of the parasitic currents is 10−310^{-3} for this problem, and since they do not disappear as the grid is refined, they can dominate in low speed simulations.

5.4 Rising bubble

The rising bubble problem has been widely used in the multiphase flow community to assess the space–time accuracy and robustness of the methods [45, 23, 7]. The problem follows the trajectory of a bubble submerged in a heavier fluid as it rises. We consider the domain (x,y)∈[0,1]×[0,2]\left(x,y\right)\in[0,1]\times[0,2], and a circular bubble with center in (0.5,0.5)(0.5,0.5) and diameter 0.50.5. The bubble is approximated with the initial condition,

c⁡(x,y,0)=1−12​(tanh⁡(−2​(r−0.25)ε)+1),r=(x−0.5)2+(y−0.5)2,c(x,y;0)=1-\frac{1}{2}\left(\tanh\left(-\frac{2\left(r-0.25\right)}{\varepsilon}\right)+1\right),~~r=\sqrt{(x-0.5)^{2}+(y-0.5)^{2}}, (156)

and the rest of the variables are initialized to zero. We consider a Cartesian mesh with element size h=2−4h=2^{-4}, and a polynomial order N=10N=10. The physical parameters are taken from [45] and are summarized in Table 6.

We consider two tests: the first with moderate density ratio ρ1/ρ2=10\rho_{1}/\rho_{2}=10, the second with large density ratio ρ1/ρ2=1000\rho_{1}/\rho_{2}=1000. The boundary conditions are free–slip walls in x=0x=0 and x=1x=1, and no–slip walls in y=0y=0 and y=2y=2. For the Test 1, the chemical characteristic time is not big enough to use the explicit Runge–Kutta, and we use the second order IMEX BDF method, with time–step Δ​t=7.2⋅10−6\Delta t=7.2\cdot 10^{-6}. For the Test 2, we use the explicit third order Runge–Kutta, with Δ​t=7.2⋅10−7\Delta t=7.2\cdot 10^{-7}. Although we use fixed time–stepping, in both cases the CFL number (CFL=16​(N+1)​(|u|+a)​Δ​t\mathrm{CFL}=16(N+1)\left(|u|+a\right)\Delta t) is maintained close to 0.2.

Although the model presented in this paper is diffuse interface, we compare it to a sharp interface model. Moreover, in this test case we compare the artificial compressibility method to a pressure–correction method that enforces the incompressible constraint in a transient simulation. Thus, we can assess the validity of the model and its implementation.

The shape of the bubble at the final time t=3.0t=3.0 is represented in Fig. 5. First, in Fig. 5(a), we represent the final shape of the interface by drawing three contour lines: c=0.1c=0.1 in dash–dot, c=0.5c=0.5 as a solid line, and c=0.9c=0.9 as a dashed line. The sharp interface reference solution is represented with black dots. We find a good agreement in both the position and the shape of the bubble, as the c=0.5c=0.5 contour follows the shape of the bubble, and the dots are always found inside the c=0.1c=0.1 and c=0.9c=0.9 contours. Next, in Fig. 5(b) we represent the concentration contour, with the velocity vectors on top. The solution obtained is also in agreement with other diffuse interface works [7].

In Fig. 6 we represent the evolution of the center of gravity (Fig. 6(a)) and the bubble rise velocity (Fig. 6(b)),

Xc=1A​∑e⟨𝒥⁡(1−C),X⟩E,N,Vc=1A​∑e⟨𝒥⁡(1−C),U⟩E,N,A=∑e⟨𝒥⁡(1−C),1⟩E,N.X_{c}=\frac{1}{A}\sum_{e}\left\langle\mathcal{J}(1-C),X\right\rangle_{E,N},~~V_{c}=\frac{1}{A}\sum_{e}\left\langle\mathcal{J}(1-C),U\right\rangle_{E,N},~~A=\sum_{e}\left\langle\mathcal{J}(1-C),1\right\rangle_{E,N}. (157)

Both center of gravity position and rise velocity show good agreement with the sharp interface reference. As for the rise velocity in Fig. 6(b), the oscillations are a result of the artificial compressibility pressure waves. One can reduce the amplitude of these oscillations by increasing the artificial sound speed c0c_{0}, but we have only found small differences in the evolution when increasing this parameter above the value used here.

Next, we solve the more challenging rising bubble Test 2 (see Table 6) with a higher density (ρ1/ρ2=1000\rho_{1}/\rho_{2}=1000) and viscosity (μ1/μ2=100\mu_{1}/\mu_{2}=100) ratios. The evolution of the bubble and the flow configuration are represented in Fig. 7 at each 0.50.5 second.

Both the shape and position of the bubble are in agreement with the sharp interface method [45], and other diffuse interface Cahn–Hilliard solvers [7]. Contrary to the rising bubble Test 1, the bubble now leaves behind an elongated skirt, which influences the velocity field. For completeness, we represent the center of gravity position and rise velocity as a function of time in Fig. 8, compared to the sharp interface solution provided in [45].

Compared to the sharp interface reference, there are visible differences. However, it has been noted in [45, 7] that the solution with different sets of equations might differ for this more challenging test case. Nonetheless, the evolution of the center of gravity and the rise velocity presented here agree with other diffuse interface solvers [7].

5.5 Three–dimensional annular flow simulation

The last numerical experiment we present is a three–dimensional flow in a straight pipe (L=10L=10) with circular section (D=1D=1). Depending on the flow rates of fluid 1 and 2, the flow regime can be of different nature: stratified, slug, dispersed bubble, and annular. The last is the one we compute here, where one of the fluids behaves as a coating around the pipe surface. More details of the flow can be found in [46, 47].

We construct a zz–oriented mesh of the pipe with 8200 elements, and use a polynomial order N=3N=3 (for both solutions and physical boundary representation). Note that this is the first time in this work that we use an unstructured curvilinear mesh. The cross section of the mesh is represented in Fig. 10(c). The physical parameters are taken from the literature [46] and given in Table 7.

For the inflow and outflow boundary conditions, we construct auxiliary ghost states,

𝐐i​n=(ci​nρ⁡(ci​n)​u→i​np),𝐐o​u​t=(cρ​u→0),\mathbf{Q}^{in}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}c_{in}\\ \sqrt{\rho\left(c_{in}\right)}\svec{u}_{in}\\ p\end{array}\right),~~\mathbf{Q}^{out}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}c\\ \sqrt{\rho}\svec{u}\\ 0\end{array}\right), (158)

with

ci​n=12+12​tanh⁡(x−x0ε+110​sin⁡(10​z)+110​sin⁡(20​y)),ui​n=0,vi​n=0,wi​n=(V1​ci​n+V2​(1−ci​n))​(1−4​x2+y2D2),pi​n=0.\begin{split}c_{in}&=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\tanh\left(\frac{x-x_{0}}{\varepsilon}+\frac{1}{10}\sin\left(10z\right)+\frac{1}{10}\sin\left(20y\right)\right),\\ u_{in}&=0,\\ v_{in}&=0,\\ w_{in}&=\left(V_{1}c_{in}+V_{2}\left(1-c_{in}\right)\right)\left(1-4\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{D^{2}}\right),\\ p_{in}&=0.\end{split} (159)

Furthermore, we use 𝐐i​n\mathbf{Q}^{in} as the initial condition. The velocities V1V_{1} and V2V_{2}, and interface position x0x_{0} are set so that the superficial velocities, defined as,

Vs​1=1π​R2​∫inletV1​ci​n​(1−4​x2+y2D2)​⁡𝑑S,Vs​2=1π​R2​∫inletV2​(1−ci​n)​(1−4​x2+y2D2)​⁡𝑑S,V_{s1}=\frac{1}{\pi R^{2}}\int_{\mathrm{inlet}}V_{1}c_{in}\left(1-4\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{D^{2}}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S,~~V_{s2}=\frac{1}{\pi R^{2}}\int_{\mathrm{inlet}}V_{2}(1-c_{in})\left(1-4\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{D^{2}}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S, (160)

are those found in [46]. Precisely, we chose the velocities Vs​1=4.9V_{s1}=4.9 m/s and Vs​2=0.06V_{s2}=0.06 m/s, which produce the annular flow regime. If we place the interface between both fluids at x0=−0.262x_{0}=-0.262 m (which yields a slip velocity V1−V2=10V_{1}-V_{2}=10 m/s), the inlet velocities are V1=11.06V_{1}=11.06 m/s and V2=1.06V_{2}=1.06 m/s. At the walls, we also impose a contact angle θw=45o\theta_{w}=45^{o}. With this configuration, we can use the third order Runge–Kutta scheme as time integrator with Δ​t=10−5\Delta t=10^{-5}. In this simulation, we take into account the effect of gravity, which points in the negative xx–direction.

The annular flow configuration is reached through an unstable mode, which makes the transient problem under–resolved until this mode is non–linearly damped and the final annular flow configuration is found. For that reason, we use a non–zero penalty parameter, β\beta, on the Cahn–Hilliard equation. Precisely, we use the definition (108) with κβ=1\kappa_{\beta}=1. Otherwise, we have found the scheme to be stable, but the solution obtained is mostly noise (i.e. it is not accurate). The introduction of the penalty parameter enhances the accuracy when the flow is under–resolved [48].

We represent snapshots of the initial stages of the flow in Fig. 9. The fluid 2 is represented (c⩽0.5c\leqslant 0.5), and colored by the vertical velocity (along the xx–axis, uu). We see that in the initial steps there is an unstable mode that grows until it changes the flow configuration. The vertical velocity contour shows that when fluid 2 rises above the interface it is dragged and accelerated by the quicker fluid 1, and the contrary occurs when it is confined below the interface because of the wall. This produces a wavy pattern at t=0.3t=0.3s, which eventually wraps the fluid to the wall and produces the annular flow. In the early stages, the flow is highly under–resolved.

We represent a final snapshot for t=4.0t=4.0 s in Fig. 10, showing the contour c⩽0.5c\leqslant 0.5 (i.e. the region occupied by fluid 2), colored by the longitudinal velocity (i.e. along the zz–axis, ww).

Although the interface is flat at the inlet, the flow is unstable and breaks down into the annular flow configuration. The heavy fluid (fluid 2) is confined to the wall by the light fluid, which is introduced 82 times faster at the inlet. In Fig. 10(c) we represent the front view of the pipe, with the mesh detailed on top of it. We see that the flow gets smoother after the numerical and physical dissipation take over the mode breakdown after the under–resolved stages in Fig. 10.

6 Summary and conclusions

We have derived a two–phase flow model that combines the Cahn–Hilliard equation (3), a skew–symmetric version of the momentum equation (17), and an artificial compressibility method (18) to get the pressure. Among the many available options, the versions were chosen to satisfy an entropy inequality, (60). The entropy inequality bounds the mathematical entropy inside a finite domain Ω\Omega limited with wall boundary conditions by the entropy of the initial condition. As time marches, the mathematical entropy decreases as a result of the physical and the chemical potential dissipation.

We then constructed a DG approximation that satisfies the SBP–SAT property, which allowed us to mimic the continuous entropy analysis discretely. As is usual in a DG approximation, we had choices for the fluxes at inter–element and physical boundaries. We studied two options:

  1. 1.

    Entropy conserving, using central fluxes for the advective fluxes and the BR1 scheme for the diffusion. This choice gives a bound that discretely mimics the continuous entropy bound (60). This scheme is not of practical use, since some amount of numerical dissipation is required to provide accurate solutions when non–linear terms are present [18, 43, 49, 50]. However, it serves as a baseline model to verify the stability proofs and to obtain a dissipation–free scheme.

  2. 2.

    Entropy stable, with an exact Riemann solver for the advective fluxes and the BR1 scheme for diffusive, with additional interface dissipation for the Cahn–Hilliard equation. This scheme transforms the entropy balance to an entropy inequality in the discrete version of (60), as a result of the numerical dissipation at the inter–element faces. This scheme uses the exact Riemann solver presented in [25] for the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, with an appropriate choice of the diamond fluxes that arise from the non–conservative terms, and a modification of the discrete entropy to account for solution discontinuities in the concentration as interfacial energy in the numerical solution.

Both the scheme and the stability proofs hold for three–dimensional unstructured meshes with hexahedral curvilinear elements.

We selected two choices to march the scheme in time: an explicit third–order Runge–Kutta method, and an implicit–explicit BDF with first or second order or accuracy. The former is used when the mobility is small enough to not severely restrict the time–step size, and the latter otherwise.

We test the scheme, addressing its accuracy with a manufactured solution convergence analysis, and its robustness by initializing the flow with random initial conditions. We showed that the scheme converges spectrally as expected, and that the scheme is robust in the sense that none of one hundred simulations crashed from random initial conditions, a high density ratio (ρ2/ρ1=1000\rho_{2}/\rho_{1}=1000), and a high Reynolds number (Re=106\mathrm{Re}=10^{6}). We compared the entropy–stable scheme with the more accurate Gauss counterpart (which is not provably entropy stable) to find that the latter crashes in 30%30\% of the simulations. We also solved commonly used static and rising bubble test problems to assess the steady state and transient accuracy of the solver. Finally we challenged the method by solving a three–dimensional pipe flow in the annular regime.

Appendix A Stability analysis of the alternative artificial compressibility model

We address the stability of the second artificial compressibility model (19). Since changes with respect to the original model (18) only affect to time–derivative terms, the analysis performed for spatial terms hold in this model, and we need only include the new time–derivative terms.

A.1 Continuous entropy analysis

The entropy analysis performed in Sec. 2.1 can be extended to the second artificial compressibility method (19). If we maintain the same entropy variables, all of the steps performed for space operators hold, and only the temporal terms contraction needs to be recomputed. Doing so,

⟨𝒥​G→p,G→p,t⟩E,N=∫∂e,N(P⋆−P)​(G→p,t⋅n→)​⁡𝑑S+⟨G~→p,t,∇→ξ​P⟩E,N,\left\langle\mathcal{J}\svec{G}_{p},\svec{G}_{p,t}\right\rangle_{E,N}=\int_{\partial e,N}\left(P^{\star}-P\right)\left(\svec{G}_{p,t}\cdot\svec{n}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S+\left\langle\svec{\tilde{G}}_{p,t},\svec{\nabla}_{\xi}P\right\rangle_{E,N}, (169)

we get the time derivative terms,

⟨𝒥ℱt,1⟩E,N−∫∂e,N32σε(CtG→c⋆+Ct⋆G→c−CtG→c)⋅n→dS+⟨𝒥(12ρVt​o​t2)t,1⟩E,N+⟨𝒥(1ρ0​c02G→p),G→p,t⟩E,N−1ρ0​c02∫∂e,N(PG→p,t⋆+P⋆G→p,t−PG→p,t)⋅n→dS=⟨𝒥ℱt,1⟩E,N−∫∂e,N32σε(CtG→c⋆+Ct⋆G→c−CtG→c)⋅n→dS+⟨𝒥𝒦t,1⟩E,N+⟨𝒥(12​ρ0​c02|G→p|t2),1⟩E,N−1ρ0​c02∫∂e,N(PG→p,t⋆+P⋆G→p,t−PG→p,t)⋅n→dS=⟨𝒥ℰ2,t,1⟩E,N−∫∂e,N32σε(CtG→c⋆+Ct⋆G→c−CtG→c)⋅n→dS−1ρ0​c02∫∂e,N(PG→p,t⋆+P⋆G→p,t−PG→p,t)⋅n→dS.\begin{split}&\left\langle\mathcal{J}\mathcal{F}_{t},1\right\rangle_{E,N}-\int_{\partial e,N}\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\left(C_{t}\svec{{G}}_{c}^{\star}+C_{t}^{\star}\svec{G}_{c}-C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S+\left\langle\mathcal{J}\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho V_{tot}^{2}\right)_{t},1\right\rangle_{E,N}\\ &+\left\langle\mathcal{J}\left(\frac{1}{\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}}\svec{G}_{p}\right),\svec{G}_{p,t}\right\rangle_{E,N}-\frac{1}{\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}}\int_{\partial e,N}\left(P\svec{G}_{p,t}^{\star}+P^{\star}\svec{G}_{p,t}-P\svec{G}_{p,t}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\\ =&\left\langle\mathcal{J}\mathcal{F}_{t},1\right\rangle_{E,N}-\int_{\partial e,N}\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\left(C_{t}\svec{{G}}_{c}^{\star}+C_{t}^{\star}\svec{G}_{c}-C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S+\left\langle\mathcal{J}\mathcal{K}_{t},1\right\rangle_{E,N}\\ &+\left\langle\mathcal{J}\left(\frac{1}{2\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}}|\svec{G}_{p}|_{t}^{2}\right),1\right\rangle_{E,N}-\frac{1}{\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}}\int_{\partial e,N}\left(P\svec{G}_{p,t}^{\star}+P^{\star}\svec{G}_{p,t}-P\svec{G}_{p,t}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\\ =&\left\langle\mathcal{J}\mathcal{E}_{2,t},1\right\rangle_{E,N}-\int_{\partial e,N}\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\left(C_{t}\svec{{G}}_{c}^{\star}+C_{t}^{\star}\svec{G}_{c}-C_{t}\svec{G}_{c}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\\ &-\frac{1}{\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}}\int_{\partial e,N}\left(P\svec{G}_{p,t}^{\star}+P^{\star}\svec{G}_{p,t}-P\svec{G}_{p,t}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S.\end{split} (170)

We have now obtained the time derivative of the alternative discrete entropy ℰ2\mathcal{E}_{2} (162). The first boundary integral belongs to the Cahn–Hilliard equation and was shown not to contribute at interior faces (Sec. 4.4.3) if β=0\beta=0, and to modify the entropy if β>0\beta>0. The surface free–energy is obtained in physical boundary faces (Sec. 4.4.5). The last integral was added by the discretization of the pressure time derivative Laplacian. The contribution from interior edges with the BR1 scheme (166) is

IBT∇2pt=∑interiorfaces∫f,N(⟦P⟧​G→p,t⋆+⟦G→p,t⟧​P⋆−⟦P​G→p,t⟧)⋅n→L​𝑑S=∑interiorfaces∫f,N(⟦P⟧​{{G→p,t}}+⟦G→p,t⟧​{{P}}−⟦P​G→p,t⟧)⋅n→L​𝑑S=0.\begin{split}\mathrm{IBT}_{\nabla^{2}p_{t}}=&\sum_{{\mathrm{interior}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket\svec{G}_{p,t}^{\star}+\left\llbracket\svec{G}_{p,t}\right\rrbracket P^{\star}-\left\llbracket P\svec{G}_{p,t}\right\rrbracket\right)\cdot\svec{n}_{L}\mathrm{d}S\\ =&\sum_{{\mathrm{interior}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket\{\!\{\svec{G}_{p,t}\}\!\}+\left\llbracket\svec{G}_{p,t}\right\rrbracket\{\!\{P\}\!\}-\left\llbracket P\svec{G}_{p,t}\right\rrbracket\right)\cdot\svec{n}_{L}\mathrm{d}S\\ =&0.\end{split} (171)

For physical boundaries, we apply the homogeneous Neumann boundary condition (167), so that

PBT∇2pt=∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(PG→p,t⋆+PG→p,t−PG→p,t)⋅n→dS=∑boundaryfaces∫f,N(0+PG→p,tn→−PG→p,t)⋅n→dS=0.\begin{split}\mathrm{PBT}_{\nabla^{2}p_{t}}=&\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(P\svec{G}_{p,t}^{\star}+P\svec{G}_{p,t}-P\svec{G}_{p,t}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\\ =&\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}\left(0+P\svec{G}_{p,t}\svec{n}-P\svec{G}_{p,t}\right)\cdot\svec{n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\\ =&0.\end{split} (172)

As a result, the alternative entropy (162) satisfies a continuous bound (164), and discrete entropy law,

⁡d⁡d​t(ℰ¯2β+∑boundaryfaces∫f,Nfw(C)dS)⩽−∑e⟨𝒥(M0|G→μ|2+2η𝒮:𝒮),1⟩E,N≤0,\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t}\left(\bar{\mathcal{E}}_{2}^{\beta}+\sum_{{\mathrm{boundary}\atop\mathrm{faces}}}\int_{f,N}f_{w}(C)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}S\right)\leqslant-\sum_{e}\left\langle\mathcal{J}\left(M_{0}|\svec{G}_{\mu}|^{2}+2\eta\mathcal{S}:\mathcal{S}\right),1\right\rangle_{E,N}\leq 0, (173)

where, similarly to (149), the inequality depends on whether the ERS and or central fluxes are used, and the choice of the interface penalty parameter β\beta.

Appendix B Entropy contraction of the inviscid fluxes

We show the contraction of the inviscid fluxes (47) for the iNS/CH system. To do so, we replace the entropy variables, fluxes, and non–conservative terms,

𝐰T​(∇→⋅𝐟↔e​(𝐪)+∑m=15ϕ↔m​(𝐪)⋅∇→​wm)=μ​∇→⋅(c​u→)+12​u​∇→⋅(ρ​u​u→)+12​v​∇→⋅(ρ​v​u→)+12​w​∇→⋅(ρ​w​u→)+u→⋅∇→​p+12ρuu→⋅∇→u+12ρvu→⋅∇→v+12ρwu→⋅∇→w+cu→⋅∇→μ+p∇→⋅u→=∇→⋅((12​ρ​vt​o​t2+p+c​μ)​u→)=∇→⋅f→eℰ.\begin{split}\mathbf{w}^{T}\left(\svec{\nabla}\cdot\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{f}}_{e}\left(\mathbf{q}\right)+\sum_{m=1}^{5}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{m}\left(\mathbf{q}\right)\cdot\svec{\nabla}w_{m}\right)=&\mu\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(c\svec{u}\right)+\frac{1}{2}u\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\rho u\svec{u}\right)+\frac{1}{2}v\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\rho v\svec{u}\right)+\frac{1}{2}w\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\rho w\svec{u}\right)+\svec{u}\cdot\svec{\nabla}p\\ &+\frac{1}{2}\rho u\svec{u}\cdot\svec{\nabla}u+\frac{1}{2}\rho v\svec{u}\cdot\svec{\nabla}v+\frac{1}{2}\rho w\svec{u}\cdot\svec{\nabla}w+c\svec{u}\cdot\svec{\nabla}\mu+p\svec{\nabla}\cdot\svec{u}\\ =&\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{tot}^{2}+p+c\mu\right)\svec{u}\right)=\svec{\nabla}\cdot\svec{f}^{\mathcal{E}}_{e}.\end{split} (174)

Thus, we see that the term ∇→⋅(c​u→)\svec{\nabla}\cdot\left(c\svec{u}\right) in the Cahn–Hilliard equation cancels the capillary pressure c​∇→​μc\svec{\nabla}\mu from the momentum non–conservative terms when multiplied by their respective entropy variables. Similarly, it reveals that momentum terms from the conservative and non–conservative parts cancel each other, and that the pressure term in the momentum equation cancels the velocity divergence term by way of the artificial compressibility equation.

Appendix C Point–wise discretization

In this section we list the steps to compute the solution time derivative with the DG approximation, (93). To get the point–wise values, we replace the test function by the Lagrange polynomials li​(ξ)​lj​(η)​lk​(ζ)l_{i}\left(\xi\right)l_{j}\left(\eta\right)l_{k}\left(\zeta\right). Details on the extraction of point–wise values can be found in [35].

  1. 1.

    Compute the entropy variables, 𝐖\mathbf{W}. The first entropy variable is the chemical potential, μ\mu, which is computed from (93d) and (93c),

    𝒥i​j​k​G→c,i​j​k=(C⋆−C)i​j​k​(δi​mwi​𝒥​a→i​j​k1+δj​mwj​𝒥​a→i​j​k2+δk​mwk​𝒥​a→i​j​k3)|m=0m=N+𝒥a→1i​j​k∑m=0NDi​mCm​j​k+𝒥a→2i​j​k∑m=0NDj​mCi​m​k+𝒥a→3i​j​k∑m=0NDk​mCi​j​m𝒥i​j​k​μi​j​k=𝒥i​j​k​F0′​(Ci​j​k)−32​σ​ε​(δi​mwi​G~c,i​j​k1,⋆+δj​mwj​G~c,i​j​k2,⋆+δk​mwk​G~c,i​j​k3,⋆)|m=0m=N+32σε∑m=0N(wmwiDm​iG~c,m​j​k1+wmwjDm​jG~c,i​m​k2+wmwkDm​kG~c,i​j​m3),\begin{split}\mathcal{J}_{ijk}\svec{G}_{c,ijk}=&\left(C^{\star}-C\right)_{ijk}\left(\frac{\delta_{im}}{w_{i}}\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{1}_{ijk}+\frac{\delta_{jm}}{w_{j}}\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{2}_{ijk}+\frac{\delta_{km}}{w_{k}}\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{3}_{ijk}\right)\biggr|^{m=N}_{m=0}\\ &+\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{1}_{ijk}\sum_{m=0}^{N}D_{im}C_{mjk}+\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{2}_{ijk}\sum_{m=0}^{N}D_{jm}C_{imk}+\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{3}_{ijk}\sum_{m=0}^{N}D_{km}C_{ijm}\\ \mathcal{J}_{ijk}\mu_{ijk}=&\mathcal{J}_{ijk}F_{0}^{\prime}(C_{ijk})-\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\left(\frac{\delta_{im}}{w_{i}}{\tilde{G}}_{c,ijk}^{1,\star}+\frac{\delta_{jm}}{w_{j}}{\tilde{G}}_{c,ijk}^{2,\star}+\frac{\delta_{km}}{w_{k}}{\tilde{G}}_{c,ijk}^{3,\star}\right)\biggr|_{m=0}^{m=N}\\ &+\frac{3}{2}\sigma\varepsilon\sum_{m=0}^{N}\left(\frac{w_{m}}{w_{i}}D_{mi}{\tilde{G}}_{c,mjk}^{1}+\frac{w_{m}}{w_{j}}D_{mj}{\tilde{G}}_{c,imk}^{2}+\frac{w_{m}}{w_{k}}D_{mk}{\tilde{G}}_{c,ijm}^{3}\right),\end{split} (175)

    where Di​j=lj′​(ξi)D_{ij}=l^{\prime}_{j}(\xi_{i}) is the derivative matrix, and recall the definition of contravariant components (69). We then get the entropy variables from the current values of the state vector, 𝐐\mathbf{Q}, and the chemical potential, μ\mu computed by (175),

    𝐖i​j​k=(μ,Q2ρ,Q3ρ,Q4ρ,Q5ρ0​c02)i​j​k,ρ=ρ1​C^+ρ2​(1−C^),C^=min⁡(max⁡(C,0),1).\mathbf{W}_{ijk}=\left(\mu,\frac{Q_{2}}{\sqrt{\rho}},\frac{Q_{3}}{\sqrt{\rho}},\frac{Q_{4}}{\sqrt{\rho}},\frac{Q_{5}}{\rho_{0}c_{0}^{2}}\right)_{ijk},~~\rho=\rho_{1}\hat{C}+\rho_{2}\left(1-\hat{C}\right),~~\hat{C}=\min\left(\max\left(C,0\right),1\right). (176)
  2. 2.

    Compute the gradient of the entropy variables 𝐆↔\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{G}} from (93b),

    𝒥i​j​k​𝐆↔i​j​k=(𝐖⋆,T−𝐖T)i​j​k​(δi​mwi​𝒥​a→i​j​k1+δj​mwj​𝒥​a→i​j​k2+δk​mwk​𝒥​a→i​j​k3)|m=0m=N+𝒥a→1i​j​k∑m=0NDi​m𝐖m​j​k+𝒥a→2i​j​k∑m=0NDj​m𝐖i​m​k+𝒥a→3i​j​k∑m=0NDk​m𝐖i​j​m.\begin{split}\mathcal{J}_{ijk}\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{G}}_{ijk}=&\left(\mathbf{W}^{\star,T}-\mathbf{W}^{T}\right)_{ijk}\left(\frac{\delta_{im}}{w_{i}}\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{1}_{ijk}+\frac{\delta_{jm}}{w_{j}}\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{2}_{ijk}+\frac{\delta_{km}}{w_{k}}\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{3}_{ijk}\right)\biggr|^{m=N}_{m=0}\\ &+\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{1}_{ijk}\sum_{m=0}^{N}D_{im}\mathbf{W}_{mjk}+\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{2}_{ijk}\sum_{m=0}^{N}D_{jm}\mathbf{W}_{imk}+\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{3}_{ijk}\sum_{m=0}^{N}D_{km}\mathbf{W}_{ijm}.\end{split} (177)
  3. 3.

    Compute the state vector time derivative,

    𝒥i​j​k​𝐌¯i​j​k​⁡d​𝐐i​j​k⁡d​t+(𝐅↔e⋆−𝐅↔e+∑m=15(𝚽↔mWm)♢−𝚽↔mWm)i​j​k⋅(δi​mwi𝒥a→1i​j​k+δj​mwj𝒥a→2i​j​k+δk​mwk𝒥a→3i​j​k)|m=Nm=0+∑m=0N(Di​m𝐅~e,m​j​k1+Dj​m𝐅~e,i​m​k2+Dk​m𝐅~e,i​j​m3)+∑p=1N∑m=15(𝚽~m,i​j​k1Di​pWm,p​j​k+𝚽~m,i​j​k2Dj​pWm,i​p​k+𝚽~m,i​j​k3Dk​pWm,i​j​p)=(δi​mwi​𝐅~v,i​j​k1,⋆+δj​mwj​𝐅~v,i​j​k2,⋆+δk​mwk​𝐅~v,i​j​k3,⋆)|m=0m=N+∑m=0N(wmwiDm​i𝐅~1v,m​j​k+wmwjDm​j𝐅~2v,i​m​k+wmwkDm​k𝐅~3v,i​j​m)+𝒥i​j​k𝐒i​j​k.\begin{split}\mathcal{J}_{ijk}\underline{\mathbf{M}}_{ijk}\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathbf{Q}_{ijk}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t}&+\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}^{\star}-\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\mathbf{F}}_{e}+\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left(\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right)^{\diamondsuit}-\accentset{\,\leftrightarrow}{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}_{m}W_{m}\right)_{ijk}\cdot\left(\frac{\delta_{im}}{w_{i}}\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{1}_{ijk}+\frac{\delta_{jm}}{w_{j}}\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{2}_{ijk}+\frac{\delta_{km}}{w_{k}}\mathcal{J}\svec{a}^{3}_{ijk}\right)\biggr|^{m=N}_{m=0}\\ &+\sum_{m=0}^{N}\left(D_{im}\tilde{\mathbf{F}}_{e,mjk}^{1}+D_{jm}\tilde{\mathbf{F}}_{e,imk}^{2}+D_{km}\tilde{\mathbf{F}}_{e,ijm}^{3}\right)\\ &+\sum_{p=1}^{N}\sum_{m=1}^{5}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}_{m,ijk}^{1}D_{ip}W_{m,pjk}+\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}_{m,ijk}^{2}D_{jp}W_{m,ipk}+\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}_{m,ijk}^{3}D_{kp}W_{m,ijp}\right)\\ =&\left(\frac{\delta_{im}}{w_{i}}\tilde{\mathbf{F}}_{v,ijk}^{1,\star}+\frac{\delta_{jm}}{w_{j}}\tilde{\mathbf{F}}_{v,ijk}^{2,\star}+\frac{\delta_{km}}{w_{k}}\tilde{\mathbf{F}}_{v,ijk}^{3,\star}\right)\biggr|_{m=0}^{m=N}\\ &+\sum_{m=0}^{N}\left(\frac{w_{m}}{w_{i}}D_{mi}\tilde{\mathbf{F}}^{1}_{v,mjk}+\frac{w_{m}}{w_{j}}D_{mj}\tilde{\mathbf{F}}^{2}_{v,imk}+\frac{w_{m}}{w_{k}}D_{mk}\tilde{\mathbf{F}}^{3}_{v,ijm}\right)+\mathcal{J}_{ijk}\mathbf{S}_{ijk}.\end{split} (178)
